subtopic: REFERENCE TO REQUEST FOR DIRECT REPRESENTATION ON TREASURY BOARD ADVISORY COMMITTEE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REFERENCE TO REQUEST FOR DIRECT REPRESENTATION ON TREASURY BOARD ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I wish to direct a question to 
the Minister of Finance. Will he be good enough to inform the house what consideration the government has given and what decisions have been arrived at with respect to the request of the organized government employees for direct representation on the treasury board civil service advisory committee?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REFERENCE TO REQUEST FOR DIRECT REPRESENTATION ON TREASURY BOARD ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman gave me notice of this question, which I received just before coming in. Several bodies of organized civil servants have presented many requests for favourable consideration, all coming down to this-higher pay, more money. This is particularly true, almost wholly true, with regard to the middle and upper income brackets in the service. Very difficult questions were raised by these numerous requests and I finally felt it desirable that the government get- a little advice from some independent source, that is, from persons who had not prejudged the case one way or the other. A committee, headed by Mr. Coon of the bank of Nova Scotia, was therefore set up to advise the treasury board. As soon as that was done, organized bodies of civil servants began to press very hard for representation on that committee. I felt and feel now that since we know exactly what they want, and since they have repeatedly and very ably made their representations both orally and in writing, I should not be justified in recommending to the government that a representative of them be added to this committee. I do not intend to make any such recommendation to the government.
The specific answer is that I do not think the government as a government has given consideration to the request of the organized civil servants, because I have declined and feel that 1 must decline to recommend that a representative of the civil servants, whose views we know and have before us, should be added to a body such as we have set up for advisory purposes.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: IRON ORE
subsubtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO CLOSING OP DOMINION STEEL AND COAL PLANT IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. In the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday, February 20, there appeared a Canadian Press report stating in effect that the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation's iron ore mine at Wabana, Newfoundland, the source of most of the ore for the big steel plant at Sydney, Nova Scotia, was to be closed on February 25. In view of the serious shortage of steel for our war plants will the minister say whether he has investigated this matter and will every effort be made to see that this mine remains open?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: IRON ORE
subsubtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO CLOSING OP DOMINION STEEL AND COAL PLANT IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
The difficulty about iron ore from Wabana to serve the Dominion Steel and Coal company is one of transportation. As my hon. friend may know, three of the company's largest ore boats were sunk by enemy action last autumn. The result was that the company was forced to find ore on the mainland, and a mine was opened near Bathurst, New Brunswick. About three hundred thousand tons of ore are being shipped from that mine to Sydney. The situation at Wabana at the moment is that
500,000	tons of ore are banked there awaiting shipment, and that is the total storage capacity available. It was therefore necessary to close the mining operations, since no disposition could be found for any additional ore at this time. As soon as navigation opens ore will move again from Wabana; the government is furnishing boats for the purpose, and the mine will reopen.

speechtext:
1.	The term "Physical Volume of Business" applies to a monthly index of productive operations maintained by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. The computation is based in recent years on 66 factors expressed in terms of volume. The components are classified under mining, manufactures, construction, central electric stations, railway traffic and distribution. subtopic: STUDY BY JOINT CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE OF SOURCES OF DEFENCE REQUIREMENTS AND POST-WAR CONDITIONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STUDY BY JOINT CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE OF SOURCES OF DEFENCE REQUIREMENTS AND POST-WAR CONDITIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver South (Mr. Green) asked if I would give him a statement with regard to the matter referred to in a motion for correspondence respecting joint Canada-United States study of the North Pacific area-Alaska, Yukon territory, and northern British Columbia. I promised I would. I am happy to say I have the statement now. I had been anticipating giving the house a statement, but unfortunately did not have it with me and have just this moment received it.
The joint Canada-United States study of the north Pacific area announced on January 25, 1943, was initiated by joint economic committees of Canada and the United States. These committees were established on June 20, 1941, as a result of discussions between the governments of Canada and the United States. It was agreed:

North Pacific Area
. . . that each government will appoint a committee to meet with a committee appointed by the other and that these committees shall severally and jointly study and report to their respective governments on the possibility of-
1.	Effecting a more economic, more efficient and more coordinated utilization of the combined resources of the two countries in the production of defence requirements, to the extent that this is not now being done, and
2.	Reducing the probable post-war economic dislocation consequent upon the changes which the economy in each country is presently undergoing.
The Canadian section of the joint committee was appointed on June 20, 1941, by order in council No. 4500. The joint study of the North Pacific area sponsored by the committees falls squarely within the second part of their terms of reference. No orders in council have been passed concerning this study project and no commitments respecting it have been entered into between the two governments.
The study will be conducted under the supervision of the joint economic committees. No special committee has been set up for this purpose.
The area to be studied includes Alaska, Yukon territory and northern British Columbia. The object is to study the possibilities for the economic development of the region for the benefit of the two countries and for the welfare of the inhabitants of the area.
The study is being carried on by officials of the two governments with the assistance of officials of the government of British Columbia. Charles Camsell, Deputy Minister of Mines and Resources, Ottawa, and James C. Rettie, of the Portland office of the National Resources Planning Board, have been appointed to organize and direct the study. The immediate purpose is simply to gather basic information and to develop proposals for the consideration of the joint economic committee. On the basis of this information the committee may make recommendations to the two governments regarding desirable measures of economic cooperation for the future development of the region.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OP GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER FEBRUARY 22

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OP GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER FEBRUARY 22
speechtext:
That on and after Monday the 22nd February, 1943, to the end of the present session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence at every sitting over all -other business except introduction of bills, -questions by members and notices of motions for [DOT]the production of papers.
He said:	Hon. members will recognize
'that this motion is identical with one which has been moved at previous sessions of this house since the beginning of this war, and, I might say, is identical in its purpose and intent with similar motions which were moved in this House of Commons at the time of the last war. When Sir Robert Borden's government was in office it was felt desirable that the attention of the house should be given with as much concentration as possible to matters pertaining to the war and with as little diversion from that main purpose as possible. It was thought inadvisable for that reason to have private members' motions occupy the time of what was known as a war session of parliament.
I may say that not only has that practice been followed in this parliament, it has been followed also at Westminster, both in this war and in the last one. In the previous war private members' motions were allowed to stand over until after government business had been fully attended to. During the period of this war both Mr. Chamberlain when he was .prime minister and Mr. Churchill as prime minister have introduced similar motions at .the different sessions.
.On one or two occasions since the house -opened, I have referred to the importance of
I Mr. Mackenzie King.l
the house giving its time as exclusively as it could to the major business of the session, namely, the country's war effort and the matters immediately pertaining thereto. I would say that there are many reasons which make this procedure more or less obviously imperative. In the first place, there is the time of the house itself to be considered and which must not be diverted more than is necessary from the large questions immediately related to the war. There is also the time of the ministers. They would be obliged to remain in the house while resolutions were being called and particular resolutions were being discussed, obliged to prepare themselves in advance on subjects some of which are more or less, if not in large part, of academic interest or on subjects that might give rise to a good deal in the way of political discussion. A further consideration at this time is the services that are being rendered by members of the public service.
They are all, at least those who are at the head of departments, more or less overburdened with the additional work which has been thrown on their shoulders at this time of war. If they were also obliged to assist in the preparation of information to be used in debate on private members' resolutions, their task would be considerably augmented. I would put as of first importance the impression that would be created throughout the country if our newspapers from week to week were to record that we had had a discussion in this parliament occupying a day on some question such for example as the return to the gold standard or on some of the many other matters that appear in the names of private members.
This motion does not preclude the government at some later stage, if it is thought advisable, from taking up private members' motions; it simply postpones their consideration. As a matter of fact this motion does not go as far as the one that has been passed in the British house. The one at Westminster does not allow the appearance on the order paper of public bills other than those introduced by the government itself.
I think I need not say more on this question. I want to assure private members that there is no desire whatever on the part of the government to interfere in any way with their privileges or to abridge their rights in any way. I would feel that hon. members themselves, for the most part if not in entirety, will agree with the government that it is desirable, this year even more than in preceding years, that this House of Commons should give as much of its undivided attention as is possible to the measures that relate immediately to the war.

Precedence of Government Motions
Mr. M J. COLDWELL (Rosetown-Biggar): Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that while I have no objections - I am speaking as a private member-to the government taking the time that is necessary to discuss government business, I do want to register a protest lest this become a part of our procedure. Perhaps the problem could be met by having an agreement in the house that the government may take private members' days when urgent business so requires, but will leave us other private members' days when business is not so urgent. There are occasions when government business lags to some extent, and at such times it seems to me that private members' days should be permitted.
The Prime Minister cited the example of Westminster. May I remind him that the procedure at Westminster is somewhat different. They have opportunities to bring problems to the attention of the government and for brief discussion in the house on the motion for adjournment; we do not have that privilege. With regard to questions, you, sir, are very careful to compel private members to place them on the order paper. At Westminster an hour is given to questions every day. During this period many supplementary questions are asked and problems are presented to the government which really are not properly questions to be answered. In this way many matters are brought before the government by private members.
The order paper contains many important resolutions placed there by private members. Because I anticipated this motion I did not place on the order paper one that I had in mind. Hon. members consider these to be worth while, and it is our opinion that they are not merely of academic interest. We have such subject matters as pensions for widows of enlisted men of the great war; soldiers' life insurance; old age pensions; prairie farm rehabilitation and irrigation; the single transferable vote; fuel resources; farm labour shortage; the development of mineral resources; irrigation projects; wheat; power development; housing and slum clearance; soldier land settlement; agricultural commodity marketing boards; measures for rehabilitation, and so on. As I say, these topics are not of academic interest alone; they are of great public interest and give hon. members an opportunity of doing what there are few opportunities to do, namely, placing before the house the point of view not only of the member but of the people with whom he is in contact.
While I realize the necessity under war conditions of utilizing some private members' days for other pressing purposes, I wish the motion had been to the effect that the government should be empowered to take private members' days when necessary, leaving us with at least the skeleton if not the reality of private members' days.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OP GOVERNMENT NOTICES OF MOTIONS AND GOVERNMENT ORDERS ON AND AFTER FEBRUARY 22
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the explanation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to this motion, which has the effect of doing away entirely with private members' days for the remainder of this session. While it is true that the government may introduce a motion later to permit the consideration of private members' resolutions, as a result of this present motion no opportunity will be given to any member of this house to use one of his most important prerogatives, namely, the private members' day.
I realize that everything connected with the war should be given precedence at this time, and there is no group more desirous and more cooperative in that regard than His Majesty's Loyal Opposition. But this motion, coming up as it does year after year, is assuming the position of a precedent. I desire to register a protest against what I believe to be an unfair invasion of the right of the private member in this house. I admit the necessity for the precedence of war business and I have shown a willingness to cooperate, but I have noticed one thing in this parliament that is strange. When we and the empire are fighting for the survival of our political and parliamentary institutions, paradoxically enough that is the time when our rights are in many cases being whittled down, with the excuse that the needs of the war make it necessary. Through this motion the Prime Minister gives the members of the house an opportunity to place before him and the government, and through them before the country, a situation which to-day is becoming altogether too prevalent, namely, the loss of the legislative function of this house. Why? -Men and women all over this dominion are asking. Why the sense of frustration which appears to have overwhelmed the members of this house? Why is it, they ask, that the things that should be done are not being done? Why is it that nine-tenths of the vital legislation affecting the welfare of the people of Canada, aside from the exigencies of war and the needs of the moment, is being passed by controllers, administrators and other officials?

Precedence oj Government Motions
The present situation is that often we in parliament have to read the newspapers or listen to the radio to learn of important changes that are taking place in the economic set-up of this dominion. Regulations are being passed day by day which could and should be considered by this parliament, many of them resulting in an unnecessary interference with private rights and too often substituting the caprice of individual controllers for the considered judgment of the members of the House of Commons. Too often our legislative function is overriden by the executive through the passage of orders in council, increasing in volume year by year, until to-day statutes are being abrogated, amended and suspended by order in council- something that is contrary to the principles of representative government for which the Prime Minister has so long contended. It is not altogether confined to the war period; for in 1936, long before the outbreak of this war, the present government suspended the operation of a statute passed by this parliament, the wheat board act, simply by means of an order in council.
Since the war began, parliament has gradually receded in importance until now the position is such that there is little justification for the calling together of parliament, except that the government requires supply and to that end requires to impose taxation. But for purposes other than that, just look at the record on the statute book of last year and then compare it with the booklets which are being issued containing the record of the orders in council which are being passed-and I commend their issuance. Take out from the statute book divorce and other non-vital legislation and you will find that at the present time controllers control and the House of Commons has become an institution where members make speeches but where legislation no longer rests with the representatives of the people.
I ask the Prime Minister-for I know his record in espousing the rights of parliament throughout the years: can there be liberty in this land when controllers have the power to pass and are passing regulations which deny equality under the law, which result in discrimination between members of a class, which deny the right of access to the courts which should be enjoyed by all British subjects and is enjoyed to-day by the people of Great Britain? Even our greatest right- the right of habeas corpus, a right prized by all who appreciate what British justice means- has _ 'been done away with, not by act of parliament, but by one of the regulations.
 .
We have come to a position in this country -I do not want to be facetious about it- where there are so many regulations which interfere with economic laws, which overlap one another, which cannot be read consistently one with the other, and which are so impossible even for members of parliament to interpret, that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has seen fit to send letters to members of the house to explain, for instance, the rental regulations and to interpret them so that we in turn may be able to interpret to the people of Canada what the law now is as passed by controllers.
I think the time has arrived, Mr. Speaker, when we as members of this house, regardless of political persuasion, should insist on our right and privilege as members of parliament to legislate for the people of Canada, subject of course to the exception that in the interval between sessions circumstances may arise which require orders in council to be passed. Above all I do object to the infringement of economic rights, the interference with the rights of classes by orders in council while parliament is sitting. Surely the government, with its overwhelming majority in the house, can trust the members of parliament to consider legislation that is beneficial and necessary and be assured that it will be passed. On the one hand we are fighting-our men and those who are serving in the forces-for the survival of parliamentary institutions, and I think that we as members of parliament, prizing the responsibility and honour that is ours, have the right to say to the government that it has gone far enough along the road of destroying the rights of parliamentary government in this country and further it shall not go.
Our next duty is to scrutinize the accounts, to assure the people of Canada that - the money we vote will be expended fairly and honestly and secure the greatest possible results. Billions we vote and billions are expended; but what examination is there by parliament of the expenditures that are being made? The only body that we have set up for the purpose is the war expenditures committee. We have no opportunity in this chamber to examine the accounts. The estimates come down during the last week or ten days of the session and millions and tens of millions of dollars are voted in a few days without adequate consideration. When we receive the auditor general's report there is no way of breaking down the large figures which it contains.
The war expenditures committee has looked into some expenditures. I do not know exactly how many contracts have been

Precedence of Government Motions
awarded, but the number must be far in excess of 100,000. There were 86,000 last year. The war expenditures committee has been sitting throughout the period between sessions and has devoted itself to its task. I know the work of that committee; I was on it. You cannot touch the fringe in an investigation by that committee. We are supposed to scrutinize the accounts as members of parliament. The committee investigates behind closed doors; it scrutinizes behind closed doors such accounts as come before it; and then, when the matter comes before parliament, the members who comprise the committee have their lips sealed in silence. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether or not we, in allowing that condition to prevail, are discharging our responsibilities. Secrecy might be justified on the ground that to reveal the facts as they are would injure the war effort of this nation and be of benefit to the enemy. I can see no reason why their colleagues cannot be given such information in connection with overexpenditure as may come to the knowledge of the committee.
Secrecy does but one thing under these circumstances. It gives to those who would be wrongdoers, who deal with the government of Canada, through its manifold relations and departments, a false sense of security. I am not making a partisan speech. I am trying to analyse the position of members of .this parliament; for on every hand we are criticized that we are not discharging the responsibilities that are ours at this time.
As members we can secure information by asking questions. We have that opportunity on the order paper. I am not saying it is intentional, but it certainly is a coincidence, that some of the questions asked last session, dealing in the main with the situation regarding man-power, remained on the order paper long after they should have been answered. Some of them were directed as returns. Weeks and months passed by before the answers were forthcoming. Orders for returns are held up. Only last week one of the ministers-he is in the house; if he were not I would not have referred to this matter-gave an answer to a question which indicated an attitude of mind that goes much farther than any minister has gone heretofore. On February 15 the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) was asked, these questions, as reported at page 392 of Hansard. The questions were asked by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacombe):
1. Has the government taken any steps to prevent irregularities discovered in certain war industries since the beginning of the war?
The material word there is " discovered." The minister's answer was, yes. The second question was:
Has the government employed the services of chartered accountants to inquire into the operations of such companies?
The material word there is " such." The answer was, yes. The third question was:
If so, (a) when, (b) in connection with what companies, (c) with what results?
The answers admit that investigations have taken place. The answers admit that irregularities have been discovered. The answer given by the minister to the third question is this:
It is not in the public interest to give the information.
Is it not in the public interest, when the responsibility rests upon the members of this house to scrutinize expenditures, that information which is known to the government should be given to the members of this house and should not be denied them? And that answer was accepted without protest by the members of the house. We are bound under the rules by the answer that it is not in the public interest to answer. Once the answer is given no further investigation can take place so far as that question is concerned.
If we recognize the right of any member of the government to give us that answer in regard to the important question of the right of parliament to investigate expenditures, then we endanger the existence of the parliamentary system that we believe in. There are three rights-the right to legislate, the right to investigate, the right to examine. All those rights, even from the casual examination I have made, have been abrogated during the period of this parliament. I feel that members irrespective of party have had the same experience, and that we must therefore in this house, as private members, assert our rights to maintain for parliament the legislative function except in so far as the exigencies of war between sessions demand its alteration. We have a right to full and prompt information. In no other way can we hope to maintain the prestige of parliament.
There is a feeling of frustration among members which I think is general in the house. It is not lack of interest on the part of members. As to those who say that members of parliament do not work, I should like them to come to Ottawa and see the industry that is displayed by members of this house both inside and outside the house. We are denied the opportunity to do the things we were sent here to do. Too many people believe, and it is not good for public morale, that parliament is stagnant in its enterprise,

Precedence oj Government Motions
sterile in its ideas, and complacent when action is demanded. And, what is worse, they believe that the decisions of caucus are more important in the determination of Canada's policy than are debates in the House of Commons. We as members of this parliament must reassert the right of parliament to do more than vote supply.
So far as private members' days are concerned, the Prime Minister says, properly, that precedence must be given to matters of importance to the war. He mentioned that during the last war the same motion was introduced in the Canadian House of Commons.

speechtext:
Yes, pardon me; a similar motion. That is true. But in every session of parliament during the last war, private members had their days, and debated the resolutions that they had on the order paper. In 1917 private members debated such matters as pensions fluctuating in accordance with the fluctuations of prices; free entry of tractors; grants to science; the fuel situation, et cetera. In the war parliament one of the rights Sir Robert Borden endeavoured to uphold was the right of private members to express themselves as they have the opportunity to do only in untrammelled debate on their own resolutions on private members' days.
Even in 1918 it was not until March 26 that a resolution was introduced by the Prime Minister granting precedence to government business on two days in the week, Tuesday and Thursday, and it was not until about one month later, April 29, that the precedence was given to all government business. It is a singular circumstance that March 26, 1918, when private members' days were in part abridged, was one of the darkest days in our history, but even at that time the government recognized the rights of private members. A reading of Hansard of that time shows that if the right to private members' days had been interfered with or had been abrogated, there would have been strong criticism from the members of the then opposition.
The Prime Minister stated that in Great Britain they have had no private members' days since the war began. That is correct, but as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) explained, they have a right that we have not. To-day the questions before the orders of the day, and the answers were most interesting. But the ruling ordinarily is, and properly so, that you may ask only questions of current importance and

immediate interest, and you cannot continue to examine the minister questioned after his answer is given. In Great Britain a system prevails that I suggest we could adopt here and thus do away with the necessity for private members' days, giving to private members the same opportunity they would have under a resolution-that is that each day an opportunity be given for an hour or so to ask questions of the ministers of the crown in regard to their several departments, and to follow up the answers given with further questions. At Westminster private members have the opportunity of presenting their views to the government on such days as questions are permitted.
To-day Britain's parliament is at its highest level in dignity and importance and prestige. Britain's parliament epitomizes the national will, the national determination and national leadership. I make the appeal that we in this parliament individually endeavour to elevate the prestige of parliament by assuring the people of Canada that we are discharging our responsibilities, and that we have not been derelict in discharging them. The restoration of the prestige of this parliament is a vital issue.
A great deal of the criticism of parliament that one hears is not merited; none the less it exists. How are we to restore the prestige of parliament? Certainly not by formal abdication of any of our historic rights, but rather by an assertion of the independence of members of this house and a determination on the part of private members that a halt be called to the trend that is altogether too noticeable in Canada, and is increasing, almost pyramiding, as we advance through the time of the war, in detracting or subtracting from the rights of the institution of parliament. We in this parliament must put a stop to any further abdication of our rights; for experience has shown that such abdication, though voluntary, may become permanent. If we in this parliament in war time fail to assert and uphold the great principles of responsible government, the principles for which we fight, we stand in danger of losing some of these rights when peace comes.
If the Prime Minister could see his way to altering the resolution so that on the conclusion of necessary w'ar business an opportunity will be given to private members to assert their prerogative rights, this debate and the few remarks I have made would prove to have been worth while. I repeat that I speak in no partisan sense but with a desire to contribute whatever I can to raising the stature and prestige of parliament in time of war and to improving the morale of the Canadian people;

speechtext:
I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is making too sweeping a suggestion when in this fourth year of the war he proposes to sweep away the right of the ordinary member to express the views of his constituency as freely as he may wish to express them. I am told that in England the House of Commons sits continuously. I fail to see why the problems with which Canada has to deal, concerning Canada, should be any less difficult to solve than the problems with which Britain has to deal; and how we can expect to keep in close contact with the progress of affairs in Canada by sitting for only five or six months, while the British house sits throughout the year, I think requires a good deal of explanation.
I know it will be urged that we just have not the time to do all the things we wish to do. The Prime Minister says in effect: Let us get on with the war; let us keep all our attention on the war. I think everyone in this house is anxious to keep his attention on the war and to do everything necessary to further the war effort, but I believe we are falling into a serious error by neglecting what is to happen after the war. Had the Anglo-Saxon race devoted its attention a little more assiduously, in the five years preceding the war, to the matter of preparing for war, we should not have been in the precarious position we occupied during the last two or three years, and we should not be even now in such danger of defeat. In this particular age there is more danger in peace than in war. Everywhere I see indications that there are men who are designing to take away the liberties of mankind. There may be those who will laugh off that idea, but the laugh will be on the other side of their faces by and by, when they find that in their supineness they have allowed precious liberties to be filched away from them. The problems which will confront us after the armistice is signed will be far more serious in every respect than the problems which confront us now; yet up to the present time there has been hardly a half hour devoted to a discussion in this house of the problems of peace. It may be asked, how are we to know what will be the conditions confronting us when peace does come? My reply is, how were we to know what conditions would confront us after war was declared? Surely he who completely neglected provision for the war would have been well nigh a traitor to his country; and I say that those men in this
house who sit on the government benches and neglect adequate preparation for the peace are in grave danger of becoming traitors to their country.
What are we going to do about it? I fail to see how we can do anything by closing this parliament early and going home. If this parliament really governs this country; if this is really a democracy, surely we should be about the business of discussing and governing. Let me point out several of the deficiencies which are apparent to me in the conduct of our affairs. I believe this is my eighth year here, and I should like to mention some of the things on which I believe we are going wrong.
While the war is proceeding I find no means whatsoever by which members of this house may review the rulings of the various boards that infest and afflict this country. Surely if anyone should review those rules and amend or commend them, as may be found desirable, it should be the members of this house; and if the members of this house do not do it, how is it ever to be done? This parliament must devise a method of checking up on the rulings of the various boards whose actions in many cases lead me to suspect that they consist largely of irresponsible people. Sometimes I fear we have a whole group of doctrinaire playboys at work on some of these boards, drunk with the power they have been given. Yet this house has no way of checking or reviewing what is going on, or of exercising influence to prevent abuses from taking place.
Here is something else which confounds me. We have several commissions in this country, as for example the railway commission. On one occasion I ventured to suggest that the board of transport commissioners, as it is now called, was hardly conducting affairs as it ought, and I was given the impression that I had stepped into a sanctum sanctorum, a place forbidden, something like this "other place" we cannot talk about in this house. And while I am on that I want to say that I think it is an outrage that members of this house cannot refer with perfect freedom to that other chamber, and discuss what is going on there; and it seems to me that if members of this house cannot be fully informed concerning the operation of the various commissions in this country, and cannot exercise a controlling hand over them, then we have abdicated a power which parliament should possess. Yet we simply cannot afford the time to discuss any matters at all here except those which the government consider fit for us to discuss. We are treated as children, little boys who must not know too much. We may do naugthy things if we know too much. We

are not mature, we members of parliament. And as for the idea of letting the ordinary common man in Canada know about these important things which will affect every aspect of his life for the next generation, why, that would never do! He is not mature; he is not grown up or capable of forming sound judgment. How nonsensical that sounds; and all this talk about things not being in the public interest; all this suppression of public discussion in the house would seem to indicate that hon. members are not qualified to help govern this country, or that the people who sent us here are not qualified to form their own opinions.
Then there is another matter which ought to be remedied at once. There were provincial rights allowed for in the British North America Act. A good many people in Canada seem to be getting the idea that the provinces were supposed to cease to exist about the time they joined confederation. They were sovereign states before they joined, but since that time it seems to have been the consistent policy of Ottawa to weaken and destroy the rights of the provinces. Now I ask, where should the autonomy and the rights of the provinces be defended and carefully safeguarded if not in this house? Hon. members come from the various provinces, yet how often do we hear in this chamber a discussion concerning the preservation of provincial rights. It seems to me this matter ought to be given the fullest and most serious discussion. If we have arrived at a point in our history when it is unsafe to allow sovereign states, as the provinces were before they joined confederation, to exercise a full share in the governing of this country, then we all ought to know that that is so and we should be told why it is so. My own opinion is that democracy in Canada will be best preserved by full recognition of provincial rights.
I should like to see these matters discussed in the house. We have no opportunity to do it. We have now been at war three years and are into the fourth year, and during that time there have been things done with respect to the provinces which have rendered them in many respects impotent. We have seen great provinces practically taken out into the woodshed and spanked for attempting to exercise the powers which were conferred upon them by the British North America Act; and what recourse have they? Only to their own individual protests. And this house, where their cause should be defended, is not giving any time for the defence of their rights.
We have a most regrettable example within the last two or three days-the outburst from

Ontario. It may be supposed that there is no fire where all the smoke is, but I am inclined to think that there is plenty of fire. We ought to be going into these matters to protect provincial autonomy, but how are we going to do it if we are to be deprived of the right of free discussion here? The only opportunity we have is in the debate on the speech from the throne and in the budget debate.	*
I should like to refer a little further to this question of "not in the public interest". I have heard that expression until it positively nauseates me. I know it is used in Great Britain, and it is used there far too freely. "Not irr the public interest!" Imagine anything more disgusting to be said to a group of members of parliament. It may be that there are many things in the conduct of a nation's affairs which it is not advisable to make generally known throughout the country. But surely there should be provision for secret sessions, or for conferences of one kind or another, as a result of which all the essential facts pertaining to this country could be made known to every member of this house; and if it be found that any hon. member is unworthy of the trust which is placed upon him, unfit for the responsibility he carries, let him be dealt with as his constituency may see fit. But certainly all facts should be known by the members,, or at least by the leaders, so that they can be given to the members.
We in Canada do not know where we are-now. The ordinary individual throughout the country simply does not know what the position is, and the majority of the members of this house do not know. The second answer that the Prime Minister gave to the questions regarding the gold standard asked by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch)-was much more satisfactory than the first. But we read of proposals of federal union and "union now"; we hear an insistent propaganda about "united nations". I wonder why we are called "the united nations" this time, instead of "the allies", as in the last war. What does all this mean? Are we to imagine that it is accidental? What lies behind the statements of Sir Kingsley Wood with regard to an international currency and several other things? Does he just talk in his sleep when he makes remarks of that sort? What does all this mean? What do we in this house know about it? The average run of us knows pretty nearly nothing, which causes us to suspect that something pretty unsuitable is being prepared for us, something so unsavoury and unsightly that the men who are

conceiving it dare not allow it to be generally known. We see articles in the Readers' Digest and other publications which indicate what is in the minds of some of the men who are prominent in the conduct of our affairs.
I say that if we are worthy of the name of members of parliament we ought to know .about these matters. How are we to learn about them if we have not freedom of discussion? I want to know something about where we are going. Really we do not know what we are doing, because the kind of thing we bear from the government benches, and what we learn when we get out in the country, where things are actually taking place, seem to be altogether different. The whole result is to fill us with anxiety, because we are not taken into confidence and given to understand where we are going. Even though we cannot foresee what will happen day by day so far as the war is concerned, we could at least be told at what we are aiming.
I contend also that the various constituencies have a right to have their views expressed, and we should have some private members' days in order that that can be done. I suggest to the Prime Minister that some such plan as this might be worked out. I do not intend to go into details; but why not set a week, say in every three, four, or five weeks, in which the private member would have the opportunity of expressing himself? That would be playing square with the members. If we were unable to finish government business by the time at which it was desired to adjourn, the time could be extended. Why not have a temporary modification of our rules so that while private members are discussing resolutions and other matters the length of time they are permitted to speak would be reduced? An agreement might be reached by bon. members that, upon resolutions other than government business, no member could speak more than twenty minutes or perhaps ten minutes. I am certain that if we were to go to work on the problem with good will, with the desire to make our proceedings here efficient and satisfactory, we could solve this difficulty.
I have said a little more, probably, than I intended, but I think I have made it clear that I am far from satisfied regarding this matter of dispensing with private members' days. I believe this is the first occasion on which I have spoken at length on this topic, but my wrath has been accumulating during the years. I did not object to our rights being suspended for one year or two years, but when it begins to look as though the system will continue for a decade, it is high time we took account of ourselves.

That on and after Monday the 22nd February, 1943, to the end of the present session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence at every sitting over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
I am simply asking for precedence in the matter of the most important business of the country, which is the government measures relating to the war. If those measures are discussed adequately before too many months go by I see no reason why we could not make arrangements to set apart a day or two for some of the motions that appear in the names of private members and give hon. members an opportunity to discuss them. I stated at the beginning of last session that that privilege might be granted before the end of the session, but by the time we had reached the end of the session-we had had six months of it-I think most hon. members were more anxious to get back to their constituencies than they were to sit here to discuss private members' resolutions. The house is at all times master of its own business and this year will be no exception in that particular.
The government must take account of the world situation as it sees it. My. hon. friend suggests that we fix two or three days each month, but those two or three days might happen to be the worst days that our country may experience as matters may develop in the course of this war. I doubt if any of us have begun to appreciate the ordeal which this country and our armed forces may have to pass through before this year is out. Does my hon. friend know that at the present time the British house sits for only three days a week, and that only at intervals? Does he know that during the period of the blackout the British house hardly ever sits at night? Does he realize that the sessions are very brief on many occasions? Those are the facts, and yet at Westminster they manage, as my hon. friend says, with all the great world problems they have to deal with, to get through with them in a shorter period of time than we take to get through ours. Let me give the facts as I find them in Hansard on June 5, 1942, and as they appear at page 3101:
From May 21, 1940, to November .20, 1940, the British parliament had in all sixty-two sitting days. Our parliament in the complete session from May 16, 1940, to November 5, 1940, had sixty-one sitting days. The British parliament in a like period of time took one day longer than this parliament to transact its business; I think my hon. friend and all hon. members will agree that the British parliament has a much vaster programme to cover, that the questions coming up from day to day are in degree at least, if not in kind, very much more significant than some we have to consider here. For the year following, during the complete session from November 21.	1940 to
November 11, 1941, the British parliament sat 113 days in all. Here, in the complete session, from November 7, 1940 to January 21, 1942, the Canadian parliament sat during 105 days. Let me give those figures again. For the first year there were sixty-two sitting days in England as against sixty-one here. The following year, which was last year, there were 113 sitting days in Britain as against 105 in Canada. Now I come to this year. Since November 12, 1941, up to the present, the British parliament has sat for seventy-seven days. Our parliament, beginning only on January 22, not on November 12 as the British parliament did, has up to to-day sat for eighty days. In other words, we have in this time of war thus far sat this year three days longer than has the British House of Commons.
I do say that, apart altogether from the facts, it is a great mistake to estimate the amount of service which parliament renders by the length of time that members are sitting
in their places in this house. It is not the length of time they are seated; it is what hon. members say in the time they are standing. That is the important thing, and I submit that hon. members can make a much greater contribution to the effectiveness of debate by giving a good deal of time, when they are outside this House of Commons altogether, to the preparation of what they are going to say and to its condensation, and bringing the discussion to a point, than they can make by forming their judgments while discussions are in progress. It is not a matter of the numbers of words; it is the value of ideas expressed and the conviction they carry with them. That, however, is, I think, obvious.
The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has spoken about orders in council that are passed, and also about the different controls there are, the restrictions, the number of boards and the like. I do not believe there is anyone in this parliament who wishes more, with all his heart, that we could get rid of ninety per cent of the boards and one hundred per cent of some of the restrictions, than I myself. But unfortunately we are in a time of war when problems have become so large that it is not possible for the ministry as a ministry to take upon itself the administration of the many different functions, several of them wholly new-for example, the control of prices and the like-that have come up in the course of the war. These powers have to be delegated in some way to boards, but that does not mean that the ministry gives up responsibility. Unfortunately the ministry is responsible for everything that the boards do, and it is a pretty nasty responsibility on some occasions. Human nature is much the same everywhere. We have to be careful, first of all. in our selection of men, and where they make mistakes, if they do make mistakes, we must change them and try to get others who are better. But I do not think that any system of government can be devised in a time of war which, if the affairs of the country are to be properly carried on, will leave the whole burden of administration on the ministry itself and not have a considerable portion of it delegated.
As regards the numbers of orders in council, there again I think it is a false index to estimate by numbers what is being done by order in council as against what is done by parliament in legislation, because every one of these orders in council has been passed under some authority given by parliament in the first instance; and parliament, which has given that authority, can modify it or take it away at any time. It is true that a minority
Privileges and Elections

cannot do that, but after all the minority have not the responsibility of governing. The responsibility of governing has been put upon the majority by the people. A great many of these orders in council are more in the nature of records, to make sure that everything that can possibly be kept of record will be kept of record, than they are of ordinances in the way' of new legislation. And, as my hon. friend has pointed out, fairly, these orders all come before the house and are capable of being reviewed by hon. members.
I might say more on this motion but since I am anxious to have it carry I think I had better stop.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: CONSTITUENCY OF STANSTEAD-REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ORDERING NEW WRIT OF ELECTION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSTITUENCY OF STANSTEAD-REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ORDERING NEW WRIT OF ELECTION
speechtext: That pursuant to the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, which on the twenty-ninth of June, 1942, annulled for illegal practices by agents the election of Robert Greig Davidson for the electoral district of Stanstead, and in view of section 71 of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, the standing committee on privileges and elections be instructed to consider whether the house should order a new writ for an election in the said electoral district.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONSTITUENCY OF STANSTEAD-REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ORDERING NEW WRIT OF ELECTION
speechtext:
I have a brief observation or
two to make on the Prime Minister's motion, and perhaps, in prefacing my remarks, I should give the house some information regarding what has developed previously with respect to this matter. The judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada, in connection with this election case, found corrupt practices and these corrupt practices were sufficient to void the election. Section 50 of chapter 50 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, volume 2, states that, in the circumstances above-mentioned, "the election of such candidate, if he has been elected, shall be void."
In Canadian Law Reports, 1942 S.C., part V, page 319, Mr. Justice Hudson of the supreme court, hearing a motion for a stay of proceedings in this case, reviewed the steps taken. I want at this time to give to the house these particular steps as indicated in outline by the learned justice on that occasion. Mr. Justice Hudson said:
This is a motion for a stay of proceedings pending an application to the judicial committee of the privy council for special leave to appeal from a judgment of this court.
On June 26 (1942) judgment was given by this court reversing a judgment of the trial 
judges and holding that the election of the respondent to the House of Commons for Canada should be annulled. It also awarded to the petitioners the costs of their petition throughout.
On June 30, 1942, the registrar of this court certified to Your Honour as Speaker of the House of Commons the judgment and decision of the court pursuant to the provisions of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, which he cites. On the said June 30 the Speaker of the House of Commons communicated to the House of Commons the report and certificate of this court as required by the provisions of section 70 of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. On July 3, 1942, notice of this motion, the motion for a stay of proceedings, was served on the Speaker of the House of Commons and on the agent for the appellant's solicitors. I may say that the motion made before Mr. Justice Hudson was dismissed.
Sections 68, 69 and 70 of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act are set out in the judgment of Mr. Justice Hudson. Section 71 of that act reads as follows:
When the trial judges or the Supreme Court of Canada in their report on the trial of an election petition under this act, state that corrupt or illegal practices have, or that there is reason to believe that corrupt or illegal practices have extensively prevailed at the election to which the petition relates, or that they are of opinion that the inquiry into the circumstances of the election has been rendered incomplete by the action of any of the parties to the petition, and that further inquiry as to whether corrupt or illegal practices have extensively prevailed is desirable, no new writ shall issue for a new election in such cases except by order of the House of Commons.
That brings us down to the position where this motion is now moved. When this section speaks of the report of the Supreme Court of Canada it evidently means the judgment, and that is all that has been communicated to the Speaker and by the Speaker to the house. This section, however, says that no new writ shall issue for an election in such cases except by order of the House of Commons.
The point I wish to make at this moment is this, that the whole matter as to whether or not a writ of election shall issue is plainly before this house. I should like very much to have the Prime Minister explain to the house why it is necessary, on a matter which seems so very simple, to have a committee of the house appointed and set up to deal with it. I suggest to the Prime Minister that the proper thing for the government to have done and for him to have launched was a very simple resolution inviting the house to order that a writ be issued, so that we would not have before us at this time the necessity of referring the matter to the privileges and elections committee.

Privileges and Elections
Having reviewed very briefly the steps that led up to the position in which we now find ourselves, I should like the Prime Minister to explain why this procedure - is taken instead of the procedure I suggested a moment ago.

subtopic: CONSTITUENCY OF STANSTEAD-REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ORDERING NEW WRIT OF ELECTION
speechtext:
I wish to speak briefly on this motion, because I think the procedure, which I understand is an ancient procedure established by precedent and usage rather than by law, is one which probably has deprived a constituency in this -country of actual membership in this House of Commons for a considerable length of time. I believe that the house itself decided some years ago that every facility should be given to a constituency when a vacancy occurs, to elect a member. Technically there is no vacancy, I understand, until our own committee has heard the matter and made a recommendation to this house and the house has acted upon that recommendation. I rose mainly to suggest that this may deprive a *constituency of membership and representation in this house for a much longer period of time than this house, when the matter was before it some years ago, considered was either necessary or good.
I was looking up, not the law, but rather the practice as laid down on page 234 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, and if hon. members will refer to the rule and the explanatory paragraph accompanying it, it will be found, according to standing order 79:
If it shall appear that any person hath been *elected and returned a member of this house, or endeavoured so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt practices, this house will proceed with the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned in such bribery or other corrupt practices.
The explanatory note, paragraph 820, states:
This standing order has nothing to do with the different laws which fully provide for the trial and punishment of corrupt practices at elections, but it reiterates the house's privilege to deal with offences of bribery and corruption after they have been proved before the competent courts.
Then, after setting forth some of the corrupt practices, it states:
. . . the house has taken such measures as were required by law or usage or as appeared suitable to the occasion. It has been usual in such cases to order a copy of the judgment delivered by the judge and the minutes of evidence to be laid before the house.
I believe that procedure was followed in July. I wonder whether in view of parliament's desire some years ago a method should be provided to prevent a vacancy from being
prolonged because of an ancient usage, if I may put it in that way. While we should protect the privileges of the house and of members of this house, I think that when a competent court has gone into all the evidence in connection with a charge of corruption and has rendered its verdict, sustaining the charge, the seat should be declared vacant and the electors of that constituency given an opportunity to elect a new member to succeed one whose practices or, as in this case, whose agents were declared corrupt by the court.
I believe there is another ancient phase of this usage or law, into which I do not propose to go. I have seen it suggested that a constituency might be penalized by becoming ineligible to elect another member during the lifetime of this parliament. If that is the situation, then the sooner we face it the better, because to punish-for that is what it is, if we regard this parliament as we should regard it-all the people of a constituency for an offence committed by a candidate or by a few persons who surrounded the candidate is a penalty which I think should not be imposed upon a group of people of Canada in this age. We are following that usage now, but I would suggest that at some time the procedure for dealing with the matter of elections be considered and new rules laid down. Certainly I do not think any advantage should be taken of any loophole in the law which might be construed in such a way as to give a constituency a further sentence, to deny it the right of representation in this parliament to which it ought to be entitled. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and hon. members who were responsible for the revision of the election laws a few years ago would not desire to see any further penalty imposed upon the constituency of Stanstead. That was really what I wished to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister and the house, and I should like him to make some comment upon it.

subtopic: CONSTITUENCY OF STANSTEAD-REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ORDERING NEW WRIT OF ELECTION
speechtext:
As a member of the committee on privileges and elections and also a member of the committee that revised the elections act some years ago, I am rather at a loss to know what to say on this occasion. In this parliament, as in other parliaments in the past, we have a number of lawyers, and I consider that they have sadly neglected the rights of the people of Canada by permitting the present roundabout procedure to remain in the act. Of course it may be that it is because we have so many lawyers in the house that the act has been allowed to
Privileges and Elections

stand as it is at the present time. I am just an ordinary member of this house and not a lawyer; perhaps, therefore, I have something to be thankful for and some sins for which I shall not have to answer hereafter, but I should like to see the act clarified in such a way that the constituency of Stanstead or any other constituency will again not be penalized in this way. I do not believe that the hon. member who has been ousted from this house was directly responsible for what occurred, but because he is supposed to be responsible for the sins committed by those working for him. the present situation has resulted. Personally I should like to see the rights of the people protected to a greater extent than they are at present.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSTITUENCY OF STANSTEAD-REFERENCE TO STANDING COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ORDERING NEW WRIT OF ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker- my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has asked me why the government is referring this matter to the committee on privileges and elections at this time, and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) has asked me if we are using all possible expedition to see that the constituency of Stanstead, which is without a member in this house at the present time, is not unduly penalized in the matter of not being represented here.
I think I can answer both questions in one statement. This matter came before the house from His Honour Mr. Speaker on July 25, 1942; that was the first intimation the house received with respect to the judgment of the supreme court in the matter of the election at Stanstead. July 25 was a Saturday, very shortly before the adjournment of the house. At that time I consulted the proper authorities as to the course that should be pursued, and I was informed that the matter should go to the committee on privileges and elections. I so informed the house, and no exception was taken, so the matter was referred to the committee. Therefore one of the reasons that has caused me to take the action I am now taking in moving this resolution was that this house has already resolved that this question should go to the committee on privileges and elections. Unfortunately the committee did not meet before the adjournment or during the recess. At the opening of the house this year I indicated that I would take advantage of the earliest opportunity to seo that the matter was referred anew to the committee on privileges and elections to be established, and that is what I am doing now without waiting even until the address has been agreed to.

Would it not have been possible, even in the short time that was left last session, for this matter to have been dealt

with by the committee on privileges and elections?
