subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of
Justice) moved:
That a select committee of this house, consisting of the following members: Messrs. Bertrand (Laurier), Black (Yukon), Claxton, Dupuis, Hansell, Hazen, McKinnon (Kenora-Rainy River), Martin, Maybank, Michaud, McGeer, Noseworthy, Ross (Calgary), Slaght, Stirling, be appointed to consider and review the defence of Canada regulations (consolidation) 1911 and amendments thereto; with power to send for persons, papers and records; to examine witnesses under oath; and to report their opinions and observations from time to time to the house.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Before this motion is put, I should like to say a word or two. I had the honour to be a member of the committee which sat last year. It made its report on July 23. The report appears in the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons for that day.
During its sittings last year the committee went to a great deal of pains to deal with the particular matters which were brought before it. Twenty-six meetings were held; a great many witnesses were heard and many representations received. Many of these representations were on behalf of the communist party and a number of other organizations which, I believe, had been banned on account of communist affiliation. Unfortunately the adoption of the report was not moved in the house and there was no opportunity of debating it last session. Before the house adjourned I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) what the intentions of the government were with regard to implementing the recommendations of the report, particularly as to lifting the ban on the communist party. The minister's answer did not appear very satisfactory. In any event, no regard has been paid to the recommendations. It is true that, so far as I know, all the communists who were interned at that time have been released, but it seems to me that they were released under circumstances which could and would have been avoided if the recommendations of the committee had been adopted. However, the ban of illegality against the communist party is still maintained. Unlike many hon. members I am not versed in the law, but I fail to understand why the ban on the communist party should not have been lifted. The party was not illegal in this country, at least there were no legal restrictions on its activities, prior to some time in June, 1940, when it was declared illegal; and from all the information I have been able to gather, this action was taken on account of its opposition to the war.
The reason why I voted for the raising of the ban on the communist party was not that I am in accord with its policies, but that, since it had given up its opposition to the war the reason for keeping its members interned had disappeared and the party was back where it was before June, 1940. It seems to me that it would have been much better to remove the ban and put them on the same footing as they were prior to June, 1940, and I hope that either this will be done at an early date or that the house will have good reasons to the contrary.
The recommendation regarding the communist party was only one of a number of recommendations made by the committee. With regard to other organizations which had been declared illegal and whose members were prosecuted as a result of the activities they carried on, our report reads:

Defence of Canada Regulations
That subparagraph "a" of paragraph 1 of regulation 39C be amended by striking therefrom: Technocracy Incorporated, Jehovah's Witnesses, Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, International Bible Students Association, Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society Incorporated.
I understand that the three last mentioned are publishing organizations. Since this house opened, information has been placed in my hands that although the committee recommended that the ban of illegality be lifted from Jehovah's Witnesses, these people are still being prosecuted for being members of Jehovah's Witnesses. The committee was unanimously in favour of raising the ban on this particular sect, and no evidence was put before the committee by the Department of Justice which indicated that at any time Jehovah's Witnesses should have been declared an illegal organization, nor did the representatives of the department raise any objection to the recommendation made by the committee. Since coming to Ottawa, as I said, I have found that these people are still being prosecuted. Their homes are being raided and literature which they have had for ten years is being seized. There have been cases where literature forming part of private libraries has been seized, which I think is forbidden by the law. I am not versed in the law and I do not want to be, but I am told that a private library is not subject to seizure; it is only literature that is held in quantity for either sale or distribution which is subject to such action.
One case brought to my attention is that of a man named Sherwin at Cobourg, Ontario. This man's home was raided and literature which he had had in his home for ten years was seized. He was tried and convicted under sections 217 and 262 of the Customs Act. Surely a man should not be asked to say ten years later how literature had come into his possession. I doubt if many of us could remember where we got a certain book or a certain pamphlet which had been in our libraries for a number of years. I know that some years ago when certain books were declared illegal I bought as many as I could find the money with which to buy them.
In North Bay a man named William Everitt was having a hearing as a conscientious objector. In the course of his examination by the military tribunal he was asked if he was a Jehovah's Witness, and he said he was. He was then arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on the charge of being a member of an illegal organization and was sentenced to three months in gaol. A man who appeared for this organization before the committee last year, Mr. Morrell, told me that he had rented a room in his home to a woman. She went to Cleveland to attend a

convention of Jehovah's Witnesses and brought back some bibles. He told me that the Department of National Revenue informed the mounted police that she had brought these books with her. Her room was raided. But they were not content with raiding her room; they raided the rest of the house and seized several books and pamphlets which Mr. Morrell had in his possession. Not only that, they seized the brief which he had placed before the defence of Canada regulations committee during its sittings last year, or perhaps I should say the material used in preparing the brief.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Had he submitted it to the committee?

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
He had submitted it and had kept a copy, or the original. Evidently the mounted police were interested and they took it away. He told me that he has since signed a legal form to have his property returned to him. A date for a hearing was set, but after a consultation between the magistrate and the mounted police the hearing was postponed and he does not know to this day whether this material will be returned.
It seems to me that there is little use in setting up a committee of responsible members of this house to deal with questions of this kind if the government or parliament is not going to give more consideration to its report than was given to the report made by the committee of last year. It is a disgrace to the Dominion of Canada that people should be prosecuted for their religious convictions in the way in which these poor people have been prosecuted. If a committee is set up this year, I hope that the first thing it will do will be to ascertain why no attention was paid to the recommendations made last year, that is, unless the house is informed before then. I do not think I have anything further to say except that I enjoyed my work on the committee. The members were most courteous and went about their work in a businesslike way. While we did not all agree as to some parts of the report, on other parts we were unanimous. As a closing word I should like to hear some reason given why more' attention was not paid to the report made by the committee of last year.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) in connection with this motion; in fact I propose to move an amendment in a few minutes. I suggest that he widen the powers of this committee to include the subjects of naturalization and deportation.

Defence of Canada Regulations
The history of these committees on the defence of Canada regulations is probably well known to all members of the house, but at the risk of weaiying them and in order that the record may be kept straight I propose to go over some of the details of what has happened during other years in connection with these particular committees.
The first committee to study the defence of Canada regulations was set up in 1940, and members will find the motion setting up that committee on page 107 of the Journals for that year under date of June 13, 1940. I was a member of that committee, and in the course of our deliberations we found that the question of naturalization and the question of what could or could not be done after the war with people whom it might be necessary to intern, kept coming up. As a matter of fact, some witnesses were called to give evidence on these subjects. One was a senior officer of the Department of the Secretary of State, I think it was the undersecretary; he gave evidence with regard to naturalization; and another was a senior officer from the immigration branch of the Department of Mines and Resources who gave evidence on deportation. Both these witnesses are well known and of high standing and each said that some change should be made in order to meet war requirements.
The committee which met in 1940 did not have time to go into the subject fully. Their report was brought in on August 1, 1940, and it will be found on page 315 of the Journals for that year. In the report it was stated that the questions of naturalization and deportation had come up and had been partly considered. The committee made certain recommendations with regard to naturalization procedure during the war, but they went further and found as follows:
Your committee is of the opinion that measures should be taken to invest the important step of naturalization with greater solemnity and to impress upon those who apply for the privilege the importance of the obligations which they assume as British subjects.
The committee recommended that in the following session another committee should be set up which would have power to review not only the defence of Canada regulations but also the law relating to naturalization and deportation. Then in 1941, when this committee had been set up again, it was given the express power to consider questions of naturalization and deportation. The motion was passed on February 27, 1941, and will be found at page 147 of the Journals for that year. Included in the operative part of the motion we find these words:
That a select committee ... be appointed to consider and review the defence of Canada regulations (consolidation) 1940, and amendments thereto, and the law relating to naturalization and to review as well the law relating to deportation.
And so on. At the time the motion was under consideration in the house there was a discussion on these very points, and the then Secretary of State, the Hon. Mr. Casgrain, speaking on behalf of the government, said on March 3, 1941, as reported at page 1186 of Hansard of that date:
As regards solemnity in the granting of certificates of naturalization, so far as I am concerned I am of opinion that possibly later on, when the law is being amended-and this will be done only after the committee has considered the whole subject-the question might be considered of investing the procedure with more solemnity in order to impress new citizens with the obligations they assume on becoming Canadians. I give this as my personal opinion.
He went on to explain that as a result of the recommendations of the committee in 1940 an interdepartmental committee had been set up to study naturalization, but he said that the whole matter would be fully discussed during the 1941 session by the special committee of the house on the defence of Canada regulations. The intention obviously was that no changes would be made until after the question had been considered by the committee and also by the house.
The 1941 committee again heard evidence with regard to naturalization and deportation, and their report was made on June 4, 1941, and will be found at page 445 of the Journals for that year. Dealing with these two questions, the committee said:
Your committee has received some evidence and has investigated these two important subjects in part only and, notwithstanding the fact that your committee has held a great many meetings, including on occasions two meetings a day, the limited time at our command has made it impossible to devote the time to these subjects which they require in order to enable a proper report to be made to the house.
Your committee therefore respectfully begs to recommend that at the next session of tile house the law relating to naturalization and deportation and matters incidental thereto be the subject matter of a reference to a committee of the house.
Then last year, 1942, when notice was given of the setting up of a committee on the defence of Canada regulations, that part of the 1941 notice dealing with naturalization and deportation had been omitted. I complained of that at the time and asked that the committee should be authorized to consider the two subjects; I was supported in that contention by several members of the house who had served on the committee previously.

Defence of Canada Regulations
The Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) as reported at page 2100 of Hansard of 1942 took this position:
I certainly would have no objection to the committee examining any subjects.
But he went on to explain that his experience in the house and in these matters had been limited, and he thought perhaps it would be as well to let the motion go through as it stood; if the committee wished to ask for an extension of its powers it could do so. But nothing more was done. The report from the committee of 1941 was not followed either, in that no special committee was set up to deal with these two questions alone. The consequence was that nothing was done with respect to naturalization and deportation throughout the session of last year.
But now we find that on July 9, 1942, an order in council was passed which made quite important changes in the naturalization regulations, and I would remind the house through you, Mr. Speaker, that this was while parliament was still in session. One of the main changes made by this order in council was that it provided that an applicant for naturalization must file a declaration of his intention, and also provision was made that the oath of allegiance must be taken in open court.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was explaining that although two different committees of this house had recommended that the law relating to naturalization and to deportation should be further reviewed by a committee of the house and then of course dealt with by the house itself; although that has not been done; and although previous ministers had let it be understood that some such course would be followed, we find now that last summer the fMr. Green.]
government put through orders in council which changed the naturalization regulations; and last month they passed by order in council a revised set of naturalization regulations; this I submit was unfair to this parliament and is a practice that should be frowned upon by members and one that should not be followed in the future. However, the government now have an opportunity to make up for their sins of the past-some of them at any rate-and therefore I propose to move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence):
That the motion be amended by adding after the word "thereto", in the sixth line, the following words:	and the law relating to
naturalization and to deportation.
The effect of that will be that this committee which is being set up will have the power to review not only the defence of Canada regulations, but also the law having to do with naturalization and deportation.
There are several different ways in which our naturalization law could be improved. For example, some provision should be made for naturalization schools, in which our new citizens could learn something about Canada, its laws and customs, and so on, and also naturalization textbooks might be supplied. I think we might learn a good deal from the United States in the way they naturalize new citizens. Then, some provision must be made to do away with dual citizenship. On the Pacific coast we have been faced for many years with the situation that a Japanese national would take out papers and yet at the same time, under the law of Japan, he might still be a Japanese citizen. That must be stopped.
I suggest that wider powers should be given to the naturalization judges. They are quite restricted now in the questions they can ask an applicant, and they should be given wider powers. Moreover, there should be far more solemnity when we grant a certificate of naturalization. I suggest that leading citizens should be called in to take part in the ceremony. That has been done already in certain cities of Canada, and if some such plan were worked out it would do a great deal of good not only to applicants for naturalization but also to present Canadians. It might also help us to hold out the hand of friendship to our new citizens.
There are many clubs across Canada which are interested in this naturalization problem. For example, the Canadian Club, I believe, made representations to the committee which sat in 1941, and many of the service clubs are taking an interest in the matter. They

Dejence oj Canada Regulations
should be given a chance to help to work out some better method of carrying out naturalization.
With regard to the question of deportation, I have only this to say. The ministers can contradict me if I am wrong, but I understand the present position to be that a member of the nazi party in an internment camp to-day could not be sent back to Germany after the war provided he had been in Canada for a period of five years. That is ridiculous. We must change our laws so that we can deal adequately and promptly with these people once the war is over.
Both these questions are of vital importance at the present time, and therefore I am moving the amendment. The committee that is to be set up is a small committee of only fifteen members. In each year the defence of Canada regulations committee has had the reputation of being one of the best set up by the house. Their deliberations have been non-partisan and they have really done splendid work. This year there is not so much to be dealt with in connection with the regulations; the committee is being set up much earlier than last year, and there is no doubt that they could look carefully into these two questions of naturalization and deportation.
I would appeal to the ministry, despite the few hard things I have said against them on these subjects, to accept this amendment. I think it is proper to extend the powers of the committee to deal with these two questions of naturalization and deportation as well as the defence of Canada regulations.

It may be a matter of some disappointment to them, but I believe those who have been members of the committee on the defence of Canada regulations are apprised of it. In 1914 we had a great amendment to the Naturalization Act. Instead of creating Canadian citizens alone, we created British citizens. That right involved a corresponding obligation, and that obligation was recognized in this way, that in the matter of the fundamental changes of our Naturalization Act those changes would not be undertaken without first consulting with Great Britain and the other commonwealths of the empire. That will be a definite limitation on the work of the committee. To show that this has been lived up to in Great Britain, I might refer to the report contained in the Daily Telegraph and Morning Post of January 27 last. It dealt with a debate in the House of Lords. In that debate a suggestion of an amendment was proposed to the bill dealing with an important matter-and it is an important matter-of the status of married women. Lord Simon explained that the government could not make the proposed changes, as all the clauses in the present bill had been agreed with the dominions.

I am pleased indeed to hear the minister accept the amendment just presented. It gives to me a reason for the setting up of this committee. Until that amendment was presented I was at a loss to know why this committee was being set up again this year. There was a committee last year that went into most of the problems pertaining to the defence of Canada regulations. That committee brought to Ottawa large deputations of people from many places at great expense and made a very thorough examination of this problem. After due consideration they arrived at certain recommendations. Those recommendations were presented to this house, but no opportunity has been given to the house to discuss or to express its approval or disapproval of them. Yet without being given that opportunity we are asked again to-night to consent to the setting up of another committee, which I presume is to cover exactly the same ground and review exactly the same situation. I wonder what purpose the minister has in mind in asking that this committee be set up. Does he hope that a new committee will arrive at different conclusions and bring in a different set of recommendations from those brought in last year? Or are we to conclude that unless a committee of this kind can bring in recommendations which are favourable to the government, the recommendations it does bring in will receive no consideration, and that such a committee is expected to bring in recommendations which must meet with the approval of the government before they can be brought before this house for discussion and consideration.
I am not going to deal at length with the communist situation, since that has been dealt with already in this debate, but one point puzzles me and probably the minister can give us the answer. Communists were interned and the communist party was banned, I presume for the reason that they were opposed to our war effort. Communists have been released from internment, but the communist party remains banned. Will the minister explain on what ground he makes this differentiation; why there is ground for the release of communists and no ground for the lifting of the ban? I hope the minister is not deluded into thinking that by maintaining this ban he is hindering in any way the work of that party. Rather I would suggest to the minister that by keeping the ban in effect he is giving those people reason to appeal to the public on the 72537-39}
ground that they are suffering an injustice, and that they can be and are being more successful in building up their organization under those circumstances than would be the situation if the ban were lifted.
There are one or two other points on which I wish to ask for information. The matter of Jehovah's Witnesses has already been called to the attention of this house, but I think hon. members should understand that one treatment is being meted out to-day to the communists and an entirely different treatment is being meted out to Jehovah's Witnesses. Communists have been released, and so far as I know there have been no recent prosecutions. They are allowed to operate and carry on their activity under a dozen different names in this country. On the other hand, even since the recommendations of this committee were made, in fact as late as last week, the homes of those belonging to Jehovah's Witnesses have been raided by the mounted police, their literature taken and prosecutions threatened. Attention has already been drawn to the fact that in many instances the literature taken is nothing more or less than the King James version of the Bible, the only difference between the copies taken by the mounted police and those read in Christian churches in this and all other cities being that those taken by the mounted police have been printed by a certain publishing house. In every other respect they are the same as those used by the rest of us. May I ask the minister if we have reached the stage in this dominion where he and those associated with him have been given authority to determine what religious faith a man shall follow or profess in this country. Are these people being prosecuted for military reasons, for political reasons or for religious reasons? Is it because they are not good citizens? Is it because they are opposed to our war effort? The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) was the first one to refer to the committee of last session, and he took the precaution to tell the house that he did not approve the doctrines of the communists. The members of his party who followed him have not taken the same precaution. What may be inferred from that is for the house to decide.
I was a member of that committee. In connection with the different sects and isms and doctrines which were considered by the committee, I wish to say frankly that as far

Defence of Canada Regulations
as I could see from the evidence before us the institution calling itself Jehovah's Wit>-nesses was simply an over-zealous religious sect and not at all one dangerous to the carrying on of the war by Canada. The same might be said to be true of some of the other sects, but I would be astonished if any member of the committee, bearing in mind the evidence given, would say that of the institution known as communism.
Without exception the witnesses for the communists admitted that before Russia was attacked by Germany they had opposed Canada being at war with Germany. In fact, they had come to support Canada only because Germany had attacked Russia. I think it is fair to infer that if hostilities between Russia and Germany came to an end, these same communists would again be on the side of Germany and against us.
It is not fair to say that the report of the committee last year was anywhere near to being unanimous. Members of the housespeaking to-night have referred to how high-minded the committee was, what a splendid membership there was, but I think the members of this house have a better opinion of the members of the committee than had some members of the committee of certain other members. However, I must say that our differences were expressed in argument and debate; we did not descend to the tactics of the communists. If we had, the minority would have been liquidated; they would not have had any report to make.
Evidence was given of the subversive activities in Canada of the communist party. They advocated and followed those subversive tactics in this country. Their literature showed; the evidence of the witnesses showed that they were advised to stir up dissatisfaction in Canada's armed forces, to incite the members of the forces to revolt against their leaders and against their officers. They even went so far as to advise methods of sinking the ships of war of the allied nations. Yet it is said that we should put up with that conduct in Canada.
It may be that communism is tolerated in Australia and in Great Britain. In Great Britain they may be able to laugh off communism with the other soap-box orators in Hyde park, but we in Canada cannot afford to do that. We cannot afford to have a change of government by force advocated in this country. I think the Department of Justice went a long way in adopting that section of the report with reference to the releasing of men who were then in prison, and 
I compliment the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and -the department upon not going so far as to lift the loan on communism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago when the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) said that the committee had been unanimous, I thought he was speaking of the report generally and I interrupted him. From what he said later I gathered that at that time he was referring to Jehovah's Witnesses. If he means that the committee was unanimous at that time, of course I was quite incorrect to endeavour to set him right because he was right already. However, as' to whether the committee was or was not unanimous generally I think it will be observed by the house that already two members of the house have taken diametrically opposite views. I in turn perhaps will further show the house by what I say that the committee was far from being unanimous. I also was a member of that committee.
At the outset I would indicate one rather sharp difference of opinion between myself and some of the members who have spoken. It is that, while I hold strongly that certain things ought to have been done, namely, that the recommendations of the committee should have been implemented, I still do not see in the circumstances of the case, any right of recrimination such as has been demonstrated by those at the far end of the house. I do not see any occasion at all for the hon. member for Bow River, for instance, speaking in such a heated fashion about this question.
The fact of the matter is that generally speaking the committee got along much better than the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) seemed to hint in his last few words.
True, the committee was not unanimous on anything very often or for long periods of time. If the committee happened to be unanimous at a quarter to eleven o'clock, it was altogether likely that it would not be unanimous at thirteen minutes to eleven; but still the members got along well.
There is no use in private members blaming the government for the non-adoption of the report, and I do not want any person suggesting or hinting that I am an apologist for the government in this connection because they know better. Every hon. member who has spoken in this fashion knows perfectly well that there were many opportunities to have the report adopted. Every hon. member who has spoken knows that he personally had an opportunity to move the adoption of

Defence of Canada Regulations
the report, and that he refrained1 from taking the opportunity. All these members knew at every moment of the closing days of last session just where the report stood with reference to being adopted or not adopted, and they themselves had the opportunity, at any stage, of proposing the adoption of that report. And they knew they had. There is no use in blaming somebody else. It may be that somebody is to blame, but if so, blame attaches to each of them as much as to any one else.
The facts are well known as to what happened with regard to that report. The chairman of the committee was a minister of the crown. He was not in agreement with the recommendations and he did-not want to move the adoption of the report. I suppose that even if you are a minister of the crown you have some right of independence of ideas. He quit his job; he resigned as chairman; another chairman took his place, and there was considerable thought on his part and on the part of others as to whether the report should be presented for adoption as well as merely being tabled. All this is a matter of common knowledge. As far as the two groups at the far end of the chamber are concerned, they know that what I am saying is true. They had their representatives there on the committee; and not only that, they knew by conversation with other members that what I have said is entirely true. I do not approve this business of standing up and trying to blame some other person; that is why I am speaking in this way.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. McKinnon) got the approval of the members of that committee to refrain from moving the adoption of the report. It was at first his intention to move the adoption, but afterwards he called the committee together and obtained their approval to the course of simply laying the report on the table. He did not get my approval; I did not happen to be there. The hon. members who have spoken in this discussion know all this quite well. I took the view then, quite openly, that the adoption of that report should be moved, and that it was the duty of the chairman to do so. These hon. members know that, but they are trying to keep it quiet; they would like to attach the blame elsewhere.
What was the position when the chairman decided not to move the adoption of the report? It was that anybody else could move the adoption; and in pursuance of that right I put a notice on the order paper that I would do so. And then I did not do it.

speechtext:
Well, I do not know why the hon. member says "shame". I feel no particular shame about it or in telling about it afterwards; but if I were trying to hint that somebody else is to blame, I would be ashamed. Hon. members know the circumstances around the close of last session; already the house was becoming somewhat thinner. Also a certain number of people did not want to discuss this question. I have no hesitation in saying that many of my good friends from the province of Quebec urged in conversation with me that the adoption of the report should not at that particular time be moved; that the report probably would have just as much effect if it were not formally adopted. They said, and I recognized the justice of their contention, "It is going to make a division in the country at the present time; everybody is very hot about this, and we think. Maybank, if you will let it go, in the long run that will turn out to be the wiser course." I never made any secret of my position in the matter. Finally, after a lot of argument-and it took a lot, because I am a stubborn fellow-I agreed. I no sooner agreed to refrain at that time, than members of those other two groups were made aware of the fact that I was not going to move the adoption of the report, and the position was wide open for them to step in and move it themselves. But they did not do so. I am not blaming them for such decision, but one of them, at least, might have disclosed the facts rather than hint that somebody else is to blame.
These are the simple facts, and this is why the report did not happen to be adopted or its adoption did not happen to be refused. The vote on that subject would have been about as uncertain as a horse race or a general election. I do not know what would have happened, but I do know why the adoption of the report was not moved.
Every person knows that, except with respect to the recommendation relative to Technocrats and Jehovah's Witnesses, the report was by no means unanimous. In support of that statement I would remind the house it was agreed in the committee that recommendations of the committee would be kept secret until the report was tabled in the house. A completely accurate report of the doings of the committee and the report was published in the Montreal Standard within two or three days of that time. Hence everyone was informed. Many conversations were going on around the house as to what the committee was doing, and every other hon. member knew as much as the members of the committee themselves.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Shame!

Defence of Canada Regulations
I am one who believes that the report of that committee should have been implemented by the government. Make no mistake about that; that is the view I took. But I cannot agree with some lion, members who suggest that any special blame attaches to the government for the reason that the committee did not report unanimously and all members refrained from seeking adoption of the report. As a matter of fact committee opinion was fairly evenly balanced between the pros and the cons. Oh! I cannot use that expression any more on account of there being now a hyphenated party in the house; it could lead to misunderstanding. In the light of the fact that the committee was not unanimous, indeed was on a hair-spring balance, and the further fact that we did not get the house to adopt our report, I do not see how any person except one who wants to be factiously critical can, with the vehemence some hon. members have been exhibiting, lay blame on the government. It surely is quite as much their own fault. They might recall the words spoken to Brutus: The fault, dear Brutus, is in ourselves, that we are underlings.
Let me now deal with the position of some of the organizations which have been mentioned. The committee, as I said, was unanimous with regard to the Technocrats, The Technocrats are a poor little organization which, I suppose, is making some kind of study and for some reason or another they were banned. I do not imagine that there ever was any great harm in them; but when they were originally banned I was aware that there was information from societies and from companies going to the United States, which at that time was not at war. I knew of possibilities with insurance companies; I thought that something might be happening with regard to this Technocrat organization similar to what could happen with insurance companies; that information could go to the United States and be passed on to Belgium, and so forth. Information was getting from Canada to the United States and overseas from there. I thought something of the sort might be the reason for the ban. But I must say that the government never gave much of a reason for banning the Technocrats. However, I was willing for a while to let this organization stay banned. But when we came to look into the question last year, the question of whether the ban should remain on that organization or not there was no reason that anyone could suggest why it should stay banned. I think that was the view of the committee, and when they reported back to the house and the house took cognizance of it, I believe that, in the light of the facts and of the deliberations of 
the committee, the ban should have been lifted at once. I do not think there can be any argument, unless there is something that should have been told the committee-and was not told-why the ban should have been kept on that organization.
I now come to Jehovah's Witnesses. Again we must see there was unanimity in the committee's report. I have the case of the government-and of the mounted police-against Jehovah's Witnesses; and, Mr. Speaker, I would hesitate to read that case here in this house. As a matter of fact, the case against Jehovah's Witnesses, as presented to us at any rate, is just laughable. That is all there is to it. There is no occasion whatever for that organization being under the ban. I know they are a bother and, to use the language of sportdom, I wish they would take a "rain check" on their disturbances until the war is over. I understand that they go round and play phonographs in places where the phonograph records will anger those who hear them. Pretty soon a fight develops and there is a big disturbance in the community. Having done that in one community, they will do it in another. I do not say they do it all the time, but I gather they have been known to do that sort of thing. They pick out Catholic communities particularly and go and play records that damn the pope and say things against Catholics generally, and all that sort of thing. Well, if you go into any Catholic community and carry on in that way, naturally there will be trouble. But such actions do not constitute a sufficient reason to put a ban on the organization itself.
. The manner in which these people have been treated at times shows the wrong that can be done by operating under a law of this sort. Reference has already been made to the seizure of Bibles. I know of a case out in British Columbia where a considerable number of Bibles were seized and brought to a mill for destruction by reason of the fact that they were contraband and confiscated articles. The owner of the mill, looking at these Bibles, said that it was sacrilege to destroy them, and he found another use for them. Perhaps they are now in the hands of people who may read in them the proper passages from which to learn tolerance. It is nonsensical to have a law which permits such actions. As I have intimated already, the strongest case that can be made for the ban on Jehovah's Witnesses being lifted, is the very case against Jehovah's Witnesses as presented to the committee.
I now come to the position with relation to communists. I believe it is a wiser policy to lift the ban on the communists. That is the position I take with relation to them. If I

Defence of Canada Regulations
should happen to fail to remark that I am out of sympathy with the communists, I hope, sir, you will not draw from my silence any inference such as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) indicated a little time ago could be drawn from the silence of other hon. members. Perhaps, for safety's sake, I should say at once that I am not in sympathy with them and thus get out from under any possible charge. I think it is wiser to remove the ban from an organization of that sort than to drive it into underground methods. That is my whole approach to the question. I know their record was bad up to the time Russia came into the war, but I think from all we have been able to learn that such is not the situation after Russia came in. The attitude of an organization which changes because a foreign power comes in as our ally is not a satisfactory attitude. I would prefer, as all would, that they should change their attitude because of their Canadianism; nevertheless, so far as any evidence we can find is concerned, they did cease to be subversive, and as a matter of fact they are doing a great many good things throughout the country at the present time.
Now, although banned, the communists are actually organizing. They are abroad doing some kind of organizing. They are probably organizing their party, but doing it in an underground, hidden way as much as possible. They are likely, by reason of this grievance, to be doing much more harm than if they were out in the open where we could see them. After all, this country, this government, this parliament, or any of the parties in the house, need have no fear whatever of any organization which it can see. When a government drives an organization into subterranean channels, it is only inviting trouble for itself.
Moreover, we are in a decidedly illogical position. We have a law whereby people cannot belong to the communist party of Canada. As a matter of fact, they will be put in gaol or in some way detained if they belong. But we let them all out. We have a law against burglary, but we do not let out all burglars. The law forbids burglary, and if the act is done those who commit it are put in gaol. But in this case these people have all been released. Great celebrations have been held in every city, and they are appearing on platforms with other citizens and joining all sorts of other community movements; yet they and their association together with the communist party of Canada are said to be illegal. The thing is illogical.
I further think that we are in danger of creating an impression of persecution. There is danger of doing more harm in the labour 72537-40
world than any good that can be accomplished in any other way. I have observed that resolutions came in first from what one might call the extreme left wing of labour organizations; gradually they moved toward the right, and the two chief labour organizations of the country have already requested the government to lift the ban. Also a large number of other organizations have done the same. There is danger of creating a really serious grievance if some relief is not given.
There is an argument that might be presented with reference to the communists. I think the Minister of Justice might state it, namely, that this organization is illegal anyway under the criminal code. That may be so. If so, it is not made any more illegal by the ban being put on it. You cannot direct traffic any better by putting up two stop signs instead of one. If this organization is illegal under the criminal code, there is no need of this defence of Canada regulations ban.
I come now to the position of the farmer labour temple organization. This is an organization that used to own and operate a number of labour temples. The reason why it was put under the ban was that it was tinged with communism. Its officers were mostly communists. They bored from within until they got into the proper positions and there they held. I have no doubt the organization was one that propagated communism and did so successfully.
All those people who were heads of that organization have been released from internment. As far as the public can see they are honest, honourable and respected citizens going about the country. The only thing is they are not allowed to be officers of that particular organization, and in order to prevent them from becoming officers the organization has been made illegal. That is a pretty roundabout way of trying to prevent the spread of communism, and it is another example of creating a grievance and giving people a chance to talk about it all the time. It is highly illogical to leave these leaders at large; tell them they can go around making speeches here, there and everywhere, but they cannot have their labour temples, or appear in them to make speeches. It is like saying to the soap-box orator, "You may orate as much as you like, but we will kick the soap-box from under you." We take away their property, but let them loose.
There is arising in my mind a suspicion that one of the reasons for not wanting to restore this organization is that the custodian of enemy property may be in a jam. At any rate it seems so clear that there is no reason



Defence of Canada Regulations
for maintaining the ban on this organization that I am beginning to wonder whether the trustee who got the property can make a good report. I know a great deal of that property has been disposed of. I thought at one time that the custodian could take care of himself properly when he came to report on his trusteeship, but I wonder if the matter has now reached the point where it would be well to have such a report brought down and find out just what has taken place. Property difficulties should not influence us in dealing with the situation.
I know that I have spoken emphatically. I do not desire to speak with any more heat than is necessary. I do not take the position of some who have been pressing recriminatory charges against this one and that one, and the government in particular. But coolly and calmly I have reasoned the matter out to my satisfaction, and I submit to the house that it would be the part of wisdom at the present time to lift the ban from all these organizations; with respect to those concerning which the committee did not report unanimously, but with much stronger reason.-which seems to me to be unassailable-with respect to those concerning which the committee did report unanimously.	.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
As a member of the defence of Canada regulations committee of last session, which committee made a report to this house on July 23, I should like to take this opportunity of saying a few words. During the two years that I was a member of the committee I enjoyed its deliberations very much, and I must agree with those hon. members who expressed the opinion that the consideration given to the various problems by the members and the deliberations of the committee were conducted with the utmost harmony. It is true that on many points we differed radically, but on the whole I can say that all the members honestly tried to see the other person's point of view. It is a matter of considerable regret to me that I am unable to be a member of the committee this year, but I had an opportunity to take a place on the reconstruction and reestablishment committee instead of this one, and I felt that as one of the younger members of the Progressive Conservative opposition, one representing a prairie point of view and one who has taken a great deal of interest in the matter of reconstruction in the councils of our party, I should accept that opportunity and go on the reconstruction committee. For that reason I am unable to continue on the defence of Canada regulations committee this year.

Last year's committee spent a great deal of time and effort in obtaining evidence relating to the various problems with which we had to deal. As is shown by the report there were some twenty-six meetings, all extending to two hours at least. We heard witnesses from various parts of this country and from as far away as Great Britain. We had the pleasure of hearing from that great and learned jurist Sir Norman Birkett, who is a high court judge in Great Britain and who for a long time was chairman of the advisory committee under the defence regulations of the United Kingdom. I have no hesitation in telling the house that Sir Norman Birkett impressed me greatly, not only on account of his learning and undoubted ability but also on account of his broad tolerance and his personal modesty.
We held our sessions in camera, for very obvious reasons. A great deal of the evidence that was given to us could not be made public because it was confidential. I had thought that many of the deliberations of the committee were also confidential. In fact, on one occasion when we came to some conclusions it was decided unanimously by all the members of the committee that nothing would be said about what had taken place until we were readjr to table the report in this house. But to my great astonishment, within twenty-four hours after we had all decided unanimously that nobody would say anything about it the newspapers had the whole story of everything that had taken place in the committee. One would almost have thought they had a dictaphone in the room; the report was so full.
At any rate information and evidence given to us were in large measure confidential, and it seemed to me at the time and seems to me now, even in the light of the discussion that has taken place here this afternoon and evening, that it is impossible to have a properly enlightened debate in this house in connection with the matters that were dealt with for the reasons that I have given; a great deal of this large amount of evidence, which took fifty or more hours to give, was confidential, and even if it was available on an occasion like this it would be impossible to place it properly before the house and present a proper interpretation of it.
This is not a debate on the report itself but a debate on the motion to set up a new committee this year. It does seem to me, however, that in any event it would not be feasible to have a debate on the report, because statements could be made and arguments advanced, as statements have been made and arguments have been advanced this evening, which could be refuted or answered

Defence of Canada Regulations
or substantiated only by quoting from the evidence, which for obvious reasons we cannot present here. I would remind the house that as usual the committee of last year contained a large majority of government supporters. Consequently it was able to reflect government policy and, as I thought, was set up for the purpose of being of assistance to the administration. This year again, quite naturally, the committee is preponderantly composed of members on the government benches; there are ten Liberals, three Progressive Conservatives, one Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and one Social Credit.
In connection with the work of this committee I am going to suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), along the lines that have been followed by other hon. members, that before it is asked to commence its work it should be advised as to the policy of the government with respect to the report which was tabled on July 23 last. As I pointed out, practically all the time of the committee was spent in considering those points which were the subject matter of the report, in hearing the evidence and listening to the arguments, and in point of fact there was no time to deal with anything else. It does seem to me that the committee which is in the process of being set up under this motion should be told whether or not it is required to deal with those questions which were the subject matter of last year's report, or whether it is not required to do so. There would be absolutely no sense in wasting the time of that committee and the time of witnesses in going over the whole ground again, hearing the type of evidence that was heard last year and all the rest of it. unless first we knew the attitude of the administration with respect to the work done last year. I invite the Minister of Justice, who undoubtedly will close this debate, to advise us with respect to these matters so that the committee now being constituted will be fully seized of the situation, and so that its position and its work may be clarified.
One point in connection with the recommendations of the committee has not been mentioned by any of the previous speakers in this debate. It is a recommendation which has nothing to do with the matter of evidence, and consequently I feel perfectly justified in dealing with it this evening. The defence of Canada regulations as they were in force at the time our committee dealt with this matter last year contained a subsection which at the time of our deliberations was known as 39B (2), and which I think is so known in the consolidated regulations for 1942. providing as follows:
It shall be a defence to any prosecution for an offence against regulation 39 or 39A to prove that the person accused intended in good faith merely to criticize or to point out errors or defects in the government of Canada or any province thereof, or in either house of parliament of Canada or in any legislature, or in the administration of justice.
I need not read regulations 39 and 39A, but they have to do with the spreading of reports or the making of statements or utterances which are likely to cause disaffection or to prejudice the recruiting, training, discipline or administration of any of his majesty's forces. However, I would direct particular attention to the fact that in these two regulations the words used with respect to the offence are "intended or likely" to cause disaffection or prejudice recruiting and so on. The committee considered section 39B (2) very carefully and recommended to the house that the words "or the conduct of the war" be added to it. The administration has not seen fit to adopt that recommendation, and I think the house should be given a clear explanation as to why that has not been done. The position is this. There have been delivered in this house during the last three weeks speeches which, if uttered on the public platform, could render the persons making them subject to prosecution under the provisions of the defence of Canada regulations. Some of those speeches were intended to urge the administration to an even greater war effort. Some had to do with the labour situation in this country or with the armed forces. In many instances hon. members endeavoured to further a greater and better war effort; yet, if they had made their speeches on the public platforms, they might have been rendered liable to prosecution, because section 39B states:
No person shall act in any manner, spread reports, or make statements or utterances intended or likely to prejudice the recruiting, training, discipline, or administration of any of 'his majesty's forces.
If on the public platform the statement is made that Canada's war effort is not good enough; if on the public platform someone says, as hon. members have said in this house no doubt quite sincerely, that we have too many men in the armed forces and that we should reallocate our man-power, those statements might be held likely to prejudice the recruiting, discipline, training or administration of his majesty's forces, and the persons making those statements could be prosecuted. After considering this matter the committee decided that if the person making the statement could prove that he intended to act in good faith, he should not be prosecuted under these

Defence of Canada Regulations
regulations; yet for some reason which I cannot possibly understand the administration has refused to accept that recommendation. If those words were added the regulation would read like this, taking only the parts relevant to the point I am making:
It shall be a defence ... to prove that the person accused intended in good faith merely to criticize or to point out errors or defects in the conduct of the war. . . .
Surely we in this country, who are so fond of declaring Canada a free and democratic country, are entitled from a public platform, or wherever we may be, to make honest criticism of Canada's war effort, for the purpose of urging the administration to even greater efforts to bring about the defeat of our enemies.
The refusal of the administration to accept the recommendations of the committee which sat last year is nothing more or less than an attempt to continue the strangling of free speech in Canada. Unless the administration is prepared to accept this recommendation it is doing something to which the people of Canada are entirely opposed, and continuing a condition against which the united nations are fighting.
I pointed out at the beginning of my observations that the evidence before the committee was heard in camera, and I do not propose to discuss it before the house. I should, however, like to say one word in connection with a matter to which reference has been made by several other hon. members, namely, the continuation of the ban upon the sect known as Jehovah's Witnesses. I feel strongly about this matter, both as a result of what I learned from sitting on the committee and from personal knowledge respecting prosecutions in western Canada. I urge upon the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) and the administration that this matter be carefully reviewed so as to ensure that prosecutions be instituted only for the commission of some act which would be prejudicial to Canada's war effort, and that they be not instituted simply because persons are Jehovah's Witnesses.
I say this because my information is that these people are Jehovah's Witnesses by conviction. In their minds they cannot be anything else. They can be prosecuted and banned; we can do anything we like with them, but so far as they are concerned they remain Jehovah's Witnesses. This is the position which nas arisen in some instances. Five or ten people might be gathered together in a home to read the Bible. The police may come along -and I believe this has happened in certain instances-and raid the home. The occupants of the house may be charged with being Jeho-

vah's Witnesses. They appear in court, and cannot deny their being Jehovah's Witnesses because, in their own hearts and souls they believe they are Jehovah's Witnesses. It is not up to me to endeavour to interpret their feelings, because I cannot quite understand them. Nevertheless I have endeavoured to do so, and my understanding is that they have what is known as a covenant with God to be Jehovah's Witnesses, and that when they are accused of being Jehovah's Witnesses they cannot possibly appear in court and deny the allegation. Consequently a prosecution is practically tantamount to a conviction, even though they may have done nothing prejudicial to Canada's war effort. They happen to be members of a sect from which they cannot in their own minds divorce themselves.
I seconded the amendment of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and I most emphatically agree with the suggestion he made. I am pleased indeed that the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) has seen fit to adopt the suggestion. This has been a matter of considerable concern to many people across Canada over a number of years. They have felt that the whole matter of immigration and naturalization should be thoroughly convassed, and that it is the duty of members of parliament to see to it that the whole matter is reviewed.
I might point out that unless the points to which I have referred are cleared up, and if the committee is placed in a position again where it has to listen to the evidence it heard last year, it is possible it may not have time to deal with matters of naturalization and immigration. If the minister feels that the subject matter of last year's report should be considered by this year's committee, then it seems to me that the house should adopt the suggestion made by the committee which sat in 1941, namely, that a special committee be set up to consider immigration and naturalization only. We do not wish to be in a position again of having to put the matter off because the committee now to be constituted has not time to deal with it.
Many organizations in my part of the country have been giving careful consideration to naturalization, and have formulated certain ideas in connection therewith. They are anxiously awaiting the setting up of a body before which they may place their suggestions, with some hope of having them implemented. I commend the consideration given by the Secretary of State to the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South, and I certainly hope that, whether it be dealt with in the manner suggested by the hon. member or that suggested by myself, it be dealt with

Defence of Canada Regulations
in some way, and the duty we owe the country in this regard thereby discharged at this session of parliament.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I followed with considerable attention the attempt made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) to explain why the report of the committee brought in last year was not implemented. He may, or may not, have given a satisfactory explanation on technical grounds, but the fact remains that the people of the city in which I live feel very deeply in the matter, and so far as they are concerned it still stands that parliament did nothing with the report. Further, the government has done nothing with it in the interim between sessions of parliament. As I understand it, the ban on organizations such as the communist party was placed there by order in council. In other words, it could have been lifted at any time by the same process of order in council. It would have seemed to me particularly appropriate for the government to act upon the sense of the report tabled and to lift the ban, by order in council. Therefore I say that, despite the attempts of my hon. friend to explain the inaction at the last session, the fact remains that nothing has been done by parliament, or by the government he supports.
I feel I should like to underline the efforts made by other hon. members to persuade the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) to give some indication to the house and to the new committee we are now in process of setting up as to what the attitude of the administration is or will be toward any report the committee may bring in. I dare to hope that this attitude may be such as to suggest to that committee that it bring in a report very soon along the lines recommended by the committee of last year, so that at an early stage we in this house may have an opportunity of passing upon such recommendations.
I wish to join with others in making it very clear that neither I nor the members of the group to which I belong have any illusions as to the policies of the communist party or as to their attitude, shall I say, toward our political group. In the city from which I come we find ourselves competing frequently, and at times we are political enemies. So far as we are concerned, that does not matter. There is a principle at stake. We believe in the four freedoms of the Atlantic charter; we believed in them before that document was enunciated. In particular, we feel that the principle of freedom of speech is something that should be held to, not merely in an abstract form, but in actual practice and in specific cases. We
feel that this holds with respect to the communist party, particularly now that it has been demonstrated that the members of that party are not in any way against our war effort, but in fact are perhaps the most zealous in the community at the present time.
In saying a few words on this subject, particularly with reference to the communist party, I believe that I speak not so much on behalf of the communist people of the city from which I come as for the average citizens of that city, the non-communists, those who share with me a dislike of some of the policies and the strategy of the communists. I may say that the average citizen finds it difficult to understand some of the inconsistencies that obtain at the present time, a number of which have been referred to already by other speakers who have preceded me.
For example, we have the fact that this war is being fought, shall I say, for the four freedoms and for certain other freedoms as well, and yet, by maintaining this ban on the communist party and on other groups such as Jehovah's Witnesses, we deny the principle of freedom of speech. There are also some inconsistencies of another kind. The communist party is banned, but we have released from internment camps the leaders of that party. The party is banned, and yet it carries on under such other names as workers' election committee and communist labour total war committee. I have in my hand a letter from this committee which is written on a printed letterhead.
We are proud of the fact that in Ottawa there is a legation of the Soviet Union. I imagine that in the library within that legation there are works on communist economics and principles, and yet we have the spectacle of books being destroyed in this country because they have been found in the libraries of people connected with the communist party. The party is banned, and yet a great number of demonstrations are being held in this country in honour of the Soviet Union. I am thinking in particular of a large gathering which was held not long ago in Winnipeg, the theme of which was a salute to the Soviet Union. It was arranged by a committee headed by men whom we all knew to be leaders of the communist party. We were glad to cooperate with them in making it a real success. The chairman of that huge meeting was at that time a prominent citizen of Manitoba who has since been taken away, Mr. John Bracken.
These inconsistencies are rather incidental to the fact that by means of this ban we are really saying that we do not believe in freedom of speech, while at the same time that

Defence of Canada Regulations
is supposed to be one of the aims for which we are fighting. We in this group contend that to maintain such an inconsistency is definitely inimical to our war effort. From conversations which I have had with people who are non-communists, even anti-communists, I have realized that their enthusiasm for the war effort has been dampened to some extent by this very fact. They wonder what it means for the post-war period in terms oi the freedoms for which we are fighting if we cannot grant these freedoms at the present time.
We in this group have pointed out on other occasions the misgivings that many people in this country have with respect to the postwar period. One set of fears which I have encountered relates to post-war foreign policy. I find that a great many people are wondering just how long the cordial attitude which we are now displaying toward the Soviet Union will continue after the war is over. What is going to be the line-up of forces among the great powers when this conflict has come to an end and we are face to face with the question of the kind of social order we are going to have in the various countries now joined together as the united nations? Many of those to whom I have spoken have felt that this ban on the communist party indicates a desire on the part of the government to be ready, after the war is over, to suppress the ideas held and advocated by the ally that just now means so much to us in the present war.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has given the answer of this group. At the present time the Soviet Union is an ally, a major ally, of this country, and our attitude toward them at the present time is one of deep appreciation for what they are doing for us. We are also anxious that the various united nations might be able to pool their ideas after the conflict is over as to the science of economics and the ways of ordering our social life so that we may make progress. I believe that

we have some contribution to make to the social and economic life of that country, and that they can make a contribution which will be of value to us. The fear of a great many people is that the powers that be in this country do not want any infiltration into our economic life of the concepts of socialism and cooperative government to be found in some cif these other countries. The fear is, I say, that the maintenance of this ban is part of that idea; and I suggest that if this ban could be lifted this would go a long way toward helping a great many people to feel that we are thoroughly sincere in our advocacy of the four freedoms and of a new order, a better world after this war is over.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer briefly in connection with the motion calling for the setting up of this committee. I understand that a letter has been sent by the Winnipeg and district trades and labour council to the Minister of Justice, protesting strongly against the advertising which has appeared in newspapers throughout Canada, placed there by the Steel Company of Canada, and to which reference has already been made in this house. I understand that the Winnipeg and district trades and labour council has suggested-perhaps an even stronger word should be used-to the Minister of Justice that this company and, in fact, the newspapers which carried the advertising, should come in for the very close scrutiny of his department, as to whether this is not in fact subversive activity on the part of this company. I know that when the authorities, or even the defence of Canada regulations committee, go around looking for subversive activities they do not usually look in that direction, they look in the direction of groups politically to the left, or to religious sects which they cannot understand or which are out of the usual run of religious organizations. But I suggest that really subversive activity is to be found in the kind of thing which took place when that full-page advertisement appeared in all the large dailies of this country. I have received a great number of copies of this advertisement from Winnipeg, from people who were incensed by it. I emphasize the fact that the trades and labour council to which I have referred, as protesting this matter is connected with the American Federation of Labour, not with the Canadian Congress of Labour, which is the labour organization involved in the steel situation. In other words, this Winnipeg labour body is concerned with a principle. They protest the right of a large corporation to publish this advertising which slanders organized labour,

Defence of Canada Regulations
which speaks' disrespectfully of the whole principle of industrial democracy which is sacred to the workers of this dominion and which they feel is part of what this war is being fought for. I can say, from the correspondence I have had, and from the account of what took place far from Hamilton, in the city of Winnipeg in the trades and labour council last week, that the workers of this country find this kind of thing very hard to understand. In fact, despite their utmost loyalty to the war effort, despite all the offers they have made, despite their efforts to be accepted by the government as full partners in the prosecution of the war, they find their enthusiasm cooled by this sort of thing, which seems to suggest to them that all the talk about the right to organize, collective bargaining, and a better deal for labour when the war is over, does not really amount to very much. This thing, I suggest, is subversive; and if the Department of Justice or the defence of Canada regulations committee are really keen and eager to trace down subversive activity, something which is inimical to our war effort, which dampens people's enthusiasm for it, or raises questions as to the validity of the things we are fighting for, they should take some time away from chasing communists and Jehovah's Witnesses and track down this kind of thing.
I regret very much that as yet the government has not had anything to say of any consequence in this connection. One day last week the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) what he thought of this bit of advertising. I believe the reply of the Prime Minister was to the effect that he did not imagine it would make much difference what he thought. I hope that before this debate is concluded the Minister of Justice will give us some statement. Perhaps he will tell us whether he has received letters from the Winnipeg trades council, and possibly some other organizations, and will give us some statement as to whether or not his department regards such advertising as something which should go unchecked. After all, if anything of that size by way of advertising were published in the papers of this country slandering the armed forces, we know what would happen. We have in Canada a great body of working people whose sons and daughters are in the armed forces, who themselves are working hard, making their contribution to the war effort; and for them to be slandered in this way is something they feel they ought not to have to take, and something which raises questions in their minds as to what is going to happen after the war is over.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I join with others in expressing the hope that we may hear shortly from the Minister of Justice as to the desire of the government with respect to this committee. Is the government prepared for the committee to make a report fairly soon regarding lifting the ban, for example, on the communist party? I think also we should hear from the minister whether his department, or under his direction, this committee, will be given authority to track down all subversive activities, not only the kind for which they have looked so far, but the kind to which I have drawn attention in referring to the recent advertising throughout the dominion by the Steel Company of Canada.
