speechtext:
I wish to take only a minute to present a case to the minister. I am not going to traverse the ground which has already been covered by many speakers regarding the recommendations of last year's committee, but I merely ask that one aspect of this question be dealt with in the committee which I do not believe has been dealt with in years gone by. I refer to those who have been interned under the defence of Canada regulations, who are, as I understand it, allowed to have hearings before an advisory committee, and the minister on the advice of that committee decides whether or not they shall be released.
I can understand that in the early stages of the war, and particularly in the very dark days of the summer of 1940, it was better to be safe than to be sorry, and many people had to be rounded up and put out of the way where they could do no harm, until such time as we could make sure whether or not they were going to be a menace to the safety of the state. That was done in Great Britain, where many persons were rounded up who afterwards were found to be innocent. No one can blame a government for doing that when the safety of the nation is threatened, but that is now over three years ago and I

Defence of Canada Regulations
wonder whether the minister has set up any machinery for making a more careful investigation into some of these cases. I can give a particular case which I have had an opportunity of investigating at first hand, and if it is typical of others, then there are people in this country who, I am afraid, are suffering great injustice.
This is a case which I referred to the minister a considerable time ago, namely, that of a man named Alois Zieglansberger under the file number of the Department of Justice, 16-395. Here is a man who was interned on July 27, 1940. His internment number at Petawawa is P.W. 1098. This man is a British subject of German origin. Eighteen months before war was declared he and his wife were at another person's home in the northern settlements of Saskatchewan, and in the course of an argument about economic conditions in Canada, and world conditions generally, he was alleged, by the man with whom he was arguing, to have made pro-nazi statements. There were as many people there who claimed that there were no pro-nazi statements made as there were those who claimed that there had been. On the strength of information laid by the other man who was partner to the heated discussion, this man was interned on July 27, 1940. I made representations to the minister. I have a number of letters on file which I will not take the time to read. The advisory committee, on going over the case, recommended that the detention should continue. I took no further action in the matter. If the advisory committee, after examining the facts, felt that was all they could do, then there was nothing more for me to do or for the Minister of Justice.
This fall I had occasion to go into the district. This man lived at Pierceland, Saskatchewan, over a hundred miles from railway, telephone or doctor, up in the bush settlements. I went through that scattered community and talked to people of all shades of opinion. I could find no one except the particular man who laid the information who would say that the interned man had any pronazi sentiments. I found that 12S people in that scattered community, covering a considerable area, had signed a petition and sent it to the minister, assuring him that, knowing this man as they did, as a good husband and citizen and a thrifty worker, they had no doubt that there had been some miscarriage of justice.
I met the man's wife, a young woman in her twenties, with three small children, living on a Saskatchewan homestead, doing all the work herself, sawing wood, driving horses and
[Mr. T. C. Douglas.)
doing the chores. She had driven several miles in a snowstorm-the night I was there it was almost thirty degrees below zero

to come into town to see me about her husband's case. She brought her children with her because she had no one with whom to leave them. For over two years this woman has been without any support except what she could obtain with her own hands to maintain herself and her three children. I tell you, Mr Speaker, talking to that woman dressed in overalls, a man's clothing, fingernails broken, hands blistered from doing all the chores, and listening to the flimsy basis on which her husband has been held for over two years in an internment camp, I was almost ashamed of the way in which British justice, in which I had always had such great pride, was being administered in this country. I think that cases like that ought to be thoroughly investigated. They ought to be based on something more than information laid by some disgruntled individual in a community, and I should like to have some assurance from the minister tonight, now that we have more time, that machinery will be set up to go more fully into oases such as this. Compare this man's case with some others I could mention. It is no secret that in Saskatchewan the. Deutsch Bund organization was strong prior to the outbreak of the war, and I have good reason to know that. Speaking in my own constituency about the aims at world domination which Hitler had, and speaking against the Munich pact, I was warned on several occasions by officers of the Deutsch Bund that it would be a good idea to keep quiet. None of these men was interned. One was arrested one evening, but before five, o'clock next morning, he was released and he joined the army.

I want to say this in closing. I know it is not popular to espouse unpopular causes. The fact remains that as long as there are any people in this country whose liberties are being restricted, whose freedom of worship has been abrogated, whose rights and privileges are ' being interfered with, none of us are free. Even a single case like this, if it is a miscarriage of justice, this house and this committee which it is proposed to set up have a serious responsibility to see that machinery, if it is not already in existence, is set up by the Department of Justice, to examine such cases, and if these men have been unjustly interned, to have them returned to their homes, while if they are justly interned some provision should be made by the federal government to take care of their wives and dependents.

speechtext:
There is one matter that I think might well be brought to the attention of the house at this time with a view to securing from the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) a statement respecting the prosecution last June or at least the setting in motion of the wheels of prosecution against Colonel George Drew. The hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) dealt at some length with the sections of the defence of Canada regulations in question and in particular referred to sections 39 and 39A. If there is one thing that we should guard against in the use of the regulations it is that they be not used in any way by the government of the day in prosecutions that have all the appearance of political prosecutions.
The hon. member for Saskatoon City pointed out that the government had not accepted the recommendation of the committee in respect of the defences that can be raised to prosecutions under section 39, which provides that no person shall spread reports, or make statements or utterances intended or likely to cause disaffection to his majesty or act in any manner, spread reports or make statements or utterances intended or likely to prejudice recruiting ; act in any manner, spread reports or make statements or utterances, intended or likely to be prejudicial to the safety of the state or the efficient prosecution of the war.
The hon. member pointed out that the government had not accepted the recommendation made by the committee; that among the aefences that would be open to a person charged under section 39 would be that the person intended in good faith to criticize "the conduct of the war." The defence of Canada regulations are a very good example of what I was endeavouring to bring before parliament this afternoon when I criticized the government for using regulations instead of statutes of parliament. As the regulations now stand, any man in this country is liable to prosecution although his purpose is to improve the war effort of this dominion, if his words are likely to interfere with the war effort. There is not a statement that any honest, patriotic citizen could make that is likely to prejudice recruiting that cannot be construed as coming within the provisions of section 39. We saw an example of that last summer in the prosecution of George Drew. The law was set in motion, he was brought before the courts. No man in Canada, not even the Minister of Justice, who must have given permission for the starting of the action, believed that the words which were used by George Drew were not those of a patriotic Canadian citizen, a

Defence of Canada Regulations
returned soldier with a gallant record, a man whose sole purpose was to improve the Canadian war effort.
He was brought before the court. The charge was then withdrawn. If the charge had been gone ahead with and the law had been interpreted in accordance with the decision of the court of appeal of Ontario and, I believe, a decision of the court of appeal of British Columbia, however high-minded, however patriotic his intentions, however desirous he was of improving the war effort of this dominion, he was guilty of the offence if he used words that were "likely to prejudice recruiting". If the amendment suggested by the committee had been accepted by this government and the words recommended had been added to section 39B (2) a defence would have been afforded thereby. Why were those words not accepted? The time has come, I believe, when the Minister of Justice should give a full, frank, clear and definite statement to this house and the country as to the reasons for the commencement of that prosecution, as to whether the department really believed, when it permitted that prosecution to be laid, that George Drew had committed an offence akin to sedition and not far removed from treason.
The withdrawal of the charge shows clearly that the government realized that a grave mistake had been committed and a grave injustice done to Colonel Drew. The time has come when the Minister of Justice should on behalf of the government of this country state the facts, and if a mistake was made, as apparently one was, in commencing the prosecution, that an apology should be offered on behalf of the government.
The defence of Canada regulations are necessary; they must be stringent in time of war, but let it never be said that these regulations might be used for the prosecution of those who are opposed to the government. An example of the danger occurred the other day in this house when with reference to an article written by Commander MacLean, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald), after replying to the article, made the statement that at the present time the authorities were considering the prosecution of this man under the defence of Canada regulations. At that time the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) made a statement that I thought was particularly apt. His statement was that the minister had said either too much or too little. Almost a week has passed by since that statement was made by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and one begins to question whether or not once more the defence of Canada

regulations are being threatened to be used in a manner designed to prevent fair and proper criticism. They should never be used except to punish unfair and untrue criticism or criticism designed to bring or that may well bring solace to the enemy or be prejudicial to the state. I trust that the Minister of Justice when he replies will give us the facts of the Drew case. If amends should be made, as I believe they should, for the commencement of that prosecution which ended in a withdrawal on the recommendation of the special counsel employed by the crown, I hope the minister will make them by frankly admitting that a mistake was made.

speechtext:
I
should like to say a word in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and particularly to say something in regard to the solemnity of naturalization proceedings. A little over a year ago I had the good fortune to attend a United States court which was naturalizing several new Americans and making them citizens. The proceedings were extremely impressive. First the judge told them very simply what were the duties of a citizen. Each man read the United States constitution and then the declaration of independence. Each was questioned carefully on both these foundation-stones of American liberty. There was no question in my mind, or in>
the mind of the judge, that they understood what they were doing and appreciated the responsibilities of citizenship. Those men left that court imbued with a sense of patriotism and Americanism, their hearts filled with pride. We should do more to make our new citizens feel that it is a great thing to be a Canadian. So many of us seem to go about thinking it a rather shameful thing to belong to Canada. We rvant to get over that, and when these men come before the courts to take the oath of allegiance and complete the great step of becoming a citizen of this country they should be impressed with the fact that they are doing something of which they should be proud. Therefore I am pleased to support the amendment that has been moved.

speechtext:
In just a word I should like
to support the suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence), though not precisely by reason of the case mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I refer to the recommendation of the committee that an additional case for exemption be included at the end of regulation 39B. As it stands now, a person may be prosecuted under regulations

Defence oj Canada Regulations
39, 39A or 39C for making a great variety of utterances. It is a defence to any such prosecution if the person accused shows that in good faith he intended to criticize the government of Canada or its provinces, or the administration of justce. There were brought before the committee concrete cases, not the one mentioned by the hon. member for Lake Centre, of prosecutions in which there should have been a defence available to the accused on the ground stated by the committee, namely, that in good faith the accused had intended to criticize the conduct of the war.
The committee had in mind two sorts of conduct of the war. First we had in mind the conduct of the war outside Canada. A great part of the war may be conducted outside Canada by our allies, by joint boards or by various other agencies, and it should be perfectly proper for any Canadian in good faith to criticize those bodies if, in his opinion, they are affecting the conduct of the war. It was argued before the committee that in any such case the accused would have no defence provided that the prosecution found a case under regulation 39, 39A or 39C, so that for that reason this addition was suggested. There was also the additional reason that there might be some difference between the government of Canada and the agencies of the government of Canada. It might be excusable to criticize the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), but not his general staff. It might be permissible to criticize the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), though I am sure no one would wish to do so, but not the officers administering the defence of Canada regulations. It might be permitted to criticize the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), but not the contractors working for him. Therefore, to provide for those cases these words were suggested, and for the further reason that there are other agencies conducting the war in addition to the government of Canada.
When the regulation was under discussion in the committee I do not think it is a breach of confidence to say there was no objection to it. As far as I can remember we spent a good deal of time in trying to find a form of words which would meet the various cases. I do not think any formal vote was taken; certainly there was no material objection, and the proposed amendment met with the substantial support and acquiescence of the committee. We thought we were dealing with a situation which had not been contemplated at the time the regulations were drafted, that we were really making what was a drafting correction. Consequently I
hope the Minister of Justice will consider the
recommendation of the committee once more. It may be, of course, that reasons were placed before him which were not given to us as to why it should not be adopted, but certainly the committee did not hear any reasons to that effect, and I hope the minister and the government will give further consideration to the recommendation in question.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AND REVIEW REGULATIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I will be as brief and as explicit as possible in what I have to say, because I know the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) wishes to make a statement and to have the motion passed. I wish to make reference to two matters which were not discussed by the defence of Canada regulations committee last session, and my reason for mentioning them now is to bring them to the attention of the committee that is to be set up.
The first matter I desire to mention is in reference to the internment of Italians in Canada. A great deal ha9 been said about other organizations and other people who came under the defence of Canada regulations, but I think the people to whom I am referring were treated about as unjustly as anyone. In the section of the country I have the honour to represent there were about two hundred Italians picked up, but to the best of my knowledge there was very little evidence upon which infractions of the regulations could be based. For years in that section of Canada there was an acute unemployment situation, and an agitation was carried on to displace those people so as to create employment for those who were termed citizens of Canada. Upon Italy's entry into the war that was seized upon as an excuse to pick up these Italians, holus-bolus, and intern them. I knew many of those men personally, and I am reasonably sure that great injustices were perpetrated against them.
I have made representations on behalf of a few of them, and some have been released. However, others are still retained in custody, and evidently very little has been done about their cases. On two or three occasions I have brought the matter to the attention of the house. I suggest that when this committee sits some attention should be paid to the operations of the internment bureau, and special inquiries should be made as to why such a large percentage of Italians are being held in custody.
I shall not elaborate at greater length on the point, because the departmental records contain complete files of people of that nationality. I suggest, however, that the committee

Defence of Canada Regulations
should pay particular attention to this phase of the matter. Absolutely nothing was done about it at the last session of parliament, and it is for that reason I should like to bring one particular case to the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). The man I have in mind was named John Dornig, of New Waterford, Nova Scotia. He was a man of more than sixty years of age, and at the time of his internment was in poor health. During his incarceration he was under the doctor's care. A few months ago, after many representations to the department, he was released, and shortly thereafter received the following letter from the custodian of alien enemy property:
Department of the Secretary of State
Ottawa, January 29, 1913.
Dear Sir:
The custodian's out-of-pocket expenses in connection with the investigation into the administration of your affairs during your internment amounts to $100.
I shall be glad accordingly to receive a money order for this amount.
That man spent about two years in an internment camp, and while there he was ill. He lost in sickness and accident insurance about $2,500 which he would have received had he not been interned. Now, for carrying on an investigation to satisfy himself that the man was wrongly interned-and that has been proven by virtue of the fact that he was released-the custodian of alien enemy property wants him to pay $100. Surely that is something which should be examined by the committee studying the defence of Canada regulations. Some will say that the expense was incurred in connection with the administration of some of his property. I know this man has no property, and in my opinion the charge is for no reason other than that of making an examination into the files to ascertain whether or not he should be released. I leave these matters to the committee. There are cases I have been attempting to adjust by correspondence and personal representations where I am reasonably sure great injustice is being done.
There is one further matter I should like to mention. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) took considerable time to prove to the house that someone other than himself was responsible for the report of the committee not being lifted from the table. My understanding of his explanation, and my knowledge with respect to the report of the committee presented just prior to the adjournment of the house, lead me to the belief that he proved conclusively that he accepted the responsibility for the com-
[Mr. Gillis.l
mittee's report not being lifted. He stated first that he had notified Mr. Speaker in accordance with the regulations that he was prepared to move for the lifting of the report from the table. Under the regulations, after his notification no other hon. member was privileged to move for the lifting of the report. The matter stayed in abeyance in that manner until just before the adjournment of the house. I say, therefore, that if he had not notified the Speaker that he -was going to take that action, someone in this group would have done so. I believe to-night that with all his juggling of the English language with respect to the matter of lifting the report he proved conclusively that he was personally responsible for the fact that some other hon. member did not make a similar motion.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Yukon suggested that those of us who were asking that the principles of freedom of speech and freedom of assembly should be practised in war time are possibly communists. He mentioned that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) was the only member of this group who made it clear that his sympathies were not with the communist party. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) who spoke this evening was opposed at the last general election by a communist candidate. The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden) and I were opposed by officials of the communist party in Saskatchewan. I felt at that time that the communist group were following along lines which were nob in the best interest of democracy, or in the best interests of Canada and her war effort. But it seems strange that those leading officials of the communist party were permitted to stand as candidates in a general election. I did not suggest they should be interned. I believed we had a cause which could stand up to any criticism they might offer, and I am glad to say that no member of our organization endeavoured to have communist opponents placed in internment camps.
The hon. member for Yukon suggested that if hostilities between Germany and Russia came to an end, the communists would be on the side of Germany. I consider that this

Defence of Canada Regulations
does an injustice to one of our great allies, namely, Russia. Those who make statements of that kind fail to understand the fundamental differences between communism and fascism. And to suggest that those in Canada who are friends of the Soviet Union are not whole-heartedly concerned with seeing that Germany is completely defeated is simply a refusal to face facts.
I wish to voice the hope that in the near future the recommendations made last year by the committee will be acted upon by the government. I refer to the lifting of the ban on the communist party, and consideration of the status of Jehovah's Witnesses and Technocracy.

I wish to point out that this amendment is not relevant to the motion, and its acceptance may create a dangerous precedent. The amendment proposes to graft on to the motion to appoint a committee to consider and review the defence of Canada regulations, 1941, a new question, namely, the consideration of the law relating to naturalization and deportation. There is no relevancy between these two propositions. Amendments must deal with the same subject-matter as the motion they are intended to modify. A member could not, for instance, on a motion to appoint a committee to review the Criminal Code move that the committee will also review the Companies Act. The subject-matter mentioned in the notice must be strictly adhered to, or else there would be no limit and the motion to appoint a committee would open the door to all kinds of investigations of the whole administration.
I am informed that there is some agreement to accept this amendment, but I can allow it only if no exception is taken to its regularity and on condition that its adoption will not be a precedent and be binding upon me. If the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) wishes to speak he will be speaking solely on the amendment. After the amendment has been disposed of, the house will then deal with the main motion, amended or not amended as the house may decide. Then the minister may reply, but when he does so he will close the debate.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT: I expressed to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) that I had no objection to the amendment because I had discussed it with the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) and with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the absence of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). The reason why we thought it could be accepted as an amendment to the motion has been indicated in some of
the discussion here to-night. It was suggested that it might be desirable to have some provision for the possible deportation of those whom it has been found necessary to intern as enemies under the defence of Canada regulations. On account of that connection it did not strike me that the amendment was altogether foreign to the main motion. Consideration might be given as to whether or not persons whom it has been found necessary to intern under the defence of Canada regulations should be deported. For that reason the amendment might be looked upon as being connected with the main motion, and there probably would be no embarrassing precedent for Your Honour if you were to allow the amendment to be accepted.

I wish that to be noted. That is my opinion. The question is on the amendment.	'
Amendment (Mr. Green) agreed to.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am sure that hon. members will not expect me in the few minutes that remain before eleven o'clock to answer all the observations that have been made in something over three hours of debate. This is merely a motion to set up again a committee for the examination of the defence of Canada regulations. A question was addressed to the Prime Minister on February 5 by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) as to whether or not it was the intention to set up again this committee as in previous years to deal with the defence of Canada regulations. That was the first reason for the motion. The second reason was that the committee of last year recommended that it be reconstituted this year to examine the situation as it may exist at this

Defence of Canada Regulations
time. The third reason was that all the recommendations made in the report were considered. Certain of them were adopted in the forms suggested by the committee, and other modifications to the regulations were made. It was felt desirable to have the committee consider whether or not the modifications which had been made would have any effect upon the general recommendations.
One modification was dealt with by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and had to do with adding new words to section 39B of the defence of Canada regulations. This section provides that it shall be a defence to any prosecution for a violation of the section to prove that the person accused intended in good faith merely to criticize or to point out errors or defects in the government of Canada. It was suggested that the words "and the conduct of the war" should be added. This was given serious consideration, and the defence departments had serious objections to the amendment in those terms and suggested the modification which was made to regulation 16.
If and when this committee is reconstituted the officials of the defence departments will, I assume, come before the committee and explain what objections they have to the general form of the recommendation that was made. Personally I could see no serious objection to adopting that recommendation, and the law officers in the department could see no serious objection. The matter was discussed with the defence departments over a period of weeks in an effort to arrive at some formula which they considered could be inserted without danger to the safety of the state. The officers of the defence departments will be in position to give what reasons they have for the view that it would be improvident to have an amendment in those terms to section 39B.
With respect to the Jehovah's Witnesses I must say that I know nothing about them. There has not been a prosecution of Jehovah's Witnesses authorized in the department since I have been connected with it'. There was a recommendation made with respect to a large number of organizations which appeared to me to be to the effect that the regulation interfered with freedom of conscience or freedom of worship. There was inserted as an addition to paragraph 39C the following:
No person shall be guilty of an offence against this regulation by reason only of his attending a meeting, the sole purpose of which is religious Worship or instruction.

That has been added, and will be before the committee to consider whether or not it is a sufficient safeguard.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: With respect to the supposed illogical situation in which the department would be because communists have been released from custody and because the ban has not been removed, I might say that all those who have been released from custody have been released not because they were communists but because they said that they wanted to help in our war effort and because they individually signed undertakings that they would
.	.	. not participate in any propaganda or
other activities of the communist party of Canada or of any organization over which the communist party exercises control, or of any other association, group, society, or organization declared to be illegal under regulation 39C of the defence of Canada regulations.
If they have not complied with that undertaking it is not because they did not give it. They were released upon the distinct understanding and upon the assertion that they were the most ardent anti-fascists who could be found anywhere, and that they were not asking to be released for the purpose of carrying on communistic propaganda, but that they were asking to be released because they wanted to help us win the war. If instead of doing that they have done something else they have violated the undertaking. There have been certain representations that this has been done. I have had these representations investigated, and I have not yet been satisfied, with respect to any of these organizations which have been mentioned, that it would be possible to establish before a court of justice that it was an organization "over which the communist party exercises control."
As to the communist party itself and its doctrines I am not speaking for the government. I stated very clearly last year what

Dejence of Canada Regulations
my own views were. I considered that the communist party is illegal, not only because it is declared to be so in the defence of Canada regulations, but because its aims are contrary to the criminal code and because, when section 98 was struck from the criminal code, section 133 was amended by adding thereto the following:
Without limiting the generality of the meaning of the expression "seditious intention" everyone shall be presumed to have a seditious intention who publishes, or circulates any writing, printing or document in which it is advocated, or who teaches or advocates, the use, without the authority of law, of force, as a means of accomplishing any governmental change within Canada.
There is a clear distinction to be drawn between people who advocate the use of force without the authority of law as a means of accomplishing governmental changes in Canada, and the government of our Russian allies. I am quite sure that if we or any group of people from Canada were to go to Russia and to advocate the use of force to overthrow the Russian government, our organization would be looked upon in Russia as subversive and seditious.
The fact that these people have been released, or that those who adhere to their doctrines are now outspoken advocates of a substantial or total war effort, does not detract from their original aims; and quite recently language which I will quote before the committee was used by one of them at a meeting which was attended, not by persons who had been interned and released, but by others who were formerly known to be members of the communist party. And right here I may say that, at the same time that the other amendment about freedom of worship was made, regulation 39C was amended to make it an offence, not to belong to the communist party -those were the terms in which the article previously existed-but to act as a member or as an officer of the party. So that the intellectual adherence to the doctrines would not be an offence. The offence would merely be constituted by some overt act to further-the aims of the organization. The amended regulation now reads:
Every person who acts as an officer or member of an illegal organization or who advocates or defends the acts, principles or policy of such illegal organization, shall be guilty of an offence against this regulation.

Is Mr. St. Laurent, on the basis of political prejudice, to be allowed to determine what organizations and groups shall be legal or illegal in Canada? Is his personal opinion to be the measure of freedom of organization? . . . Since when does freedom of association and conscience depend upon agreements or disagreements with creeds by a minister of the crown ? . . .

That is what will be taken to be the meaning of lifting the ban in the defence of Canada regulations; and one of those who was released, Mr. Tim Buck, in a number of speeches said that what was wanted was the lifting of the ban to make the communist party a legal organization in Canada; and that if the ban were lifted, the impression throughout the country would be that something had been done by this parliament to make the communist party as legal a party as the Progressive Conservative party, to which some of the pamphlets attempt to liken it. I think that would be giving serious encouragement to propagating a doctrine which now is contrary to the criminal code, and is so under an amendment which was recognized as designed to have that effect when it was inserted in the code; because, if hon. members will look at the debate which took place in 1936, they will find Mr. Woodsworth saying to the then Minister of Justice that he was taking away with one hand what he was giving with the other by repealing section 98. And notwithstanding the logic of the reproach

Defence of Canada Regulations
that was then being made to the Minister of Justice, this house saw fit to do what the then Minister of Justice proposed, and to add to section 133 a paragraph which amounted in fact to taking away with one hand what was being given, by the repeal of section 98, as to its substantial provision, with the other hand.
